speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week CN Rail announced plans to lay off 33 per cent of its work force over the next three years. This announcement will lead to the loss of approximately 200 jobs in New Brunswick, 11 of which are in my riding of Restigouche-Chaleur.
Furthermore, there is talk of the possible abandonment of the CN line through northern New Brunswick.

I would like to express my complete disagreement with this approach. Over the past ten years, Canadian National has eliminated more than 2,000 jobs in my region, and it wants to eliminate even more. Other communities hit by severe cutbacks by CN received some kind of compensation. Although my region was promised compensation, CN has yet to deliver.

The government and CN Rail must maintain these jobs and the rail line through northern New Brunswick in order to guarantee the economic viability and development of both the region and the province.
I call upon the government and CN to immediately halt this blatant attack on rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of members the plight of residents in my community who have lost faith with Transport Canada.
Residents in my community were extremely pleased to participate last year in the hearings conducted by the environmental assessment review panel studying expansion at Pearson airport. They were encouraged by the platitudes being uttered that Transport Canada and the airport's management were all for public participation and input. They said that they wanted to keep residents involved in the future of Pearson.
Unfortunately, the government wasted their time. The residents made impassioned presentations about the unbearable levels of noise around their homes. They told of violated flight paths and jets breaking regulations by taking off in the middle of the night. They made it clear that if Transport Canada wanted to listen they had lots to say. Sadly, they were completely ignored.
The announcement of more runways makes it obvious that Transport Canada never had any intention of listening to residents in my community. It seems clear that the pattern of abuse that the airport and Transport Canada have demonstrated to my residents over the years is only going to continue.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-7 respecting the status of the artist was adopted by this House on June 11, 1992 and received royal assent on June 23 that same year. Although the legislation has yet to come into force and is therefore not

March 10, 1993
being implemented, the government is very proud of its up-to-date legislation that recognizes the status of the artist.
Because of this situation, a number of major dossiers are now on hold. This is serious, because artists' associations cannot reactivate these dossiers until the legislation is officially proclaimed, without putting the interests of the artists in jeopardy. It is high time this government stopped congratulating itself and decided to act, because it is one thing to be well intentioned and pass legislation, but another thing entirely to implement that legislation.

Mr. Speaker, free trade is working for Canada. In 1992 our merchandise exports to the U.S. surged to an all-time high of $122 billion, smashing the previous record of $110 billion set in 1990.
Every $1 billion in exports creates or maintains 15,000 jobs. Canada's exports to the U.S. increased by $31 billion in 1989-91, just after the Canada-U.S. FTA came into effect, compared to 1986-88.
According to the U.S. department of commerce, average monthly imports into the U.S. from Canada are up 25.9 per cent since the FTA, compared to the four-year period prior to the FTA.
According to Statistics Canada, 16 of 22 Canadian manufacturers increased their market share in the U.S. under the FTA.
Between 1988 and 1991 Canadian high-tech exports to the U.S. grew from $6.6 billion to $10.7 billion, which is a 63 per cent jump.

Mr. Speaker, in its report made public yesterday the national transport act review commission recommended changing the Crow benefit from a transportation policy to a payment to farmers. That payment has already been reduced by 10 per cent for the next two crop years by virtue of the December economic statement by the Minister of Finance.
Is it the government's intention to phase out the Crow benefit? If so, what is the timetable for this phase-out? Those are the questions farm people are asking.
The government should make its intentions clear. Farmers want and need money at the elevator when they deliver their grain. The government's policy thus far increases freight rates and reduces transport payments, which means that the farmer pays more to receive less for his grain.
Tell me, how does that solve the farm income crisis on the prairies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently an Ontario coroner's jury conducted an inquest into the horrifying sex slaying of Christopher Stephenson, an 11-year old boy from Brampton, Ontario. The jury produced a report which recommended that a law be established to allow sexually violent predators to be kept in prison beyond their court-imposed sentences if they are judged still to be a risk to the public.
When a sexual offender is nearing the end of his term, corrections officials should be permitted to assess whether there is a high likelihood of re-offending, and on the basis of that review decide whether the offender should remain in jail.
I understand that officials of the Department of the Solicitor General are considering proposals at this time. I would urge the minister responsible to listen to the concerns that so many Canadians have regarding public safety and introduce the appropriate legislation as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry in Nova Scotia employs approximately 27,000 people, or 7.4 per cent of the work force in my province. Of this number, over half are employed in the inshore fishing industry. It is obvious that this industry is of vital importance to Nova Scotia.
March 10, 1993

This industry suffers from declining stocks and increasing processing capacity. The Liberal Party recognizes that declining stocks are the result of foreign overfishing and bad management of quotas both within and beyond the 200-mile limit.
Those who work in the fisheries in Nova Scotia simply want to fish. They do not want to rely on government assistance. The prospective loss of employment coupled with the potential death of their communities and their way of life has many of these people worried. Something must be done.
The government must move away from short-term solutions. Greater responsibility must be taken to ensure that fish quotas are stringently observed by all parties involved, and that includes foreign fishing vessels.
The people in the fishery in my riding want to know what the future holds for them, what is going to happen to their industry down the road, and what is going to happen to them next year. They need answers and they need them now.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to voice my concerns to the House and to the government regarding the renewal of various Community Futures programs.
As the House knows, many of these programs are about to wind down as their government support comes to an end.
I can speak best of the Community Futures corporation in my area, which is the Triple S group. This group is being recommended by the department to close down, not because it has failed but because it has been successful.
I find it strange that the department wants to fund failure but fails to support success.
I call upon the minister to review the applications of second generation Community Futures funding with the strategy of endorsing success and eliminating failure.

Mr. Speaker, the latest government estimates contained many cuts. There are serious cuts to seniors, official languages, literacy and aboriginal programs.
Perhaps one of the cruelest cuts, which is often overlooked, is to foreign aid. With this particular cut contained in these estimates, $4.3 billion will have been cut from foreign aid over the last five years. Yet the government has reported that it is able to find $5.8 billion for helicopters.
This government has gone back on its promise to increase Official Development Assistance to .7 per cent of the GNP. It has now slipped to less than half of that.
The Global Village Voice reported the words of a Zambian woman. She said: "We are burying our children every day as if we were planting beans".
Priorities, priorities, what are the government's priorities?

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to continue the education of my colleague from Mississauga East in the wake of her vitriolic attack on this government's commitment to social programs.
If I had to summarize this government's activities in one word, that word would have to be groundbreaking.
For the first time in Canada we had a government that took the initiative in the fight against AIDS, that recognized the unique and so very serious reality of breast cancer, that instituted tax reform to lower the tax burden of 90 per cent of this country's senior citizens, and that initiated a nation-wide panel to confront the ever growing crisis of violence against women.
I,	for one, and the constituents of Simcoe Centre appreciate the government's efforts. In fact, over 2,000 of my constituents availed themselves of the opportunity I offered to contribute input to that panel. I wonder if my colleague can say the same.

March 10, 1993
The presence of violence and poverty in Canada is a tragedy. However, as one who is deeply concerned about social issues I would hope that in the future my colleague from Mississauga East might refrain from exploiting the disadvantaged in Canada to make partisan statements. Her constituents and all Canadians would be better served if she offered constructive solutions rather than venomous, slanted attacks.

Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court of Canada has twice confirmed the right of language minorities to manage and administer their own educational institutions.
Despite these two decisions by the highest legal authority in this country, some provinces are still dragging their feet on a matter of elementaiy educational justice that was an accepted fact nearly 12 years ago.
Since apparently these rights are closely linked to federal money, it is time the federal government sat down with the provinces, which have jurisdiction over education, and that a decision was made, once and for all.
That language minorities should have to go through all these legal contortions to defend their rights is simply intolerable. Official language minorities are asking only for recognition of their equality rights, no more and no less than the Constitution of our country guarantees: to be treated fairly and equitably without having constantly to ask.

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to thank my colleagues on the justice committee for their work during our recent hearings on crime prevention.
The culmination of the committee's work is found in our unanimous report Crime Prevention in Canada: Toward a National Strategy. We have concluded that the conventional crime control model does not work.
As Canadians are aware crime is on the increase. Many offenders are not being brought to justice and others are not being rehabilitated. Our system fails to address the underlying factors associated with crime which, if confronted, could prevent crime.
As a result Canadians live in fear as the cycles of criminal behaviour continue. Our committee has recommended a new approach to crime prevention in Canada. We must reduce opportunity for crime. We must shift our policing efforts to concentrate on the community.
We must address the social and economic conditions that breed crime. We must teach kids about crime prevention at all levels of their education, and we must provide Canadians with a means to avoid becoming involved in criminal activity.
This requires a co-ordinated effort. I am proud to have contributed to what I believe is an outstanding report. My committee colleagues and I are eagerly awaiting the response of the government to our 11 recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, long-term sustainable development in the Third World only occurs when basic human development needs are met.
Infrastructure and other advanced economic development will only happen when basic health care, nutritional, educational and training needs are fulfilled. Non-governmental organizations are by far the best vehicle for Canada to use to deliver development assistance. NGOs are ideally suited to working with counterparts in developing countries and provide tens of thousands of Canadians with opportunities for direct involvement in development work both in Canada and abroad.
Despite all this the government has so lost touch with the reality of international development that it has decided yet again to slash support to Canadian non-governmental organizations. Instead of undermining their
March 10, 1993

Oral Questions
development work the government ought to be asking NGOs to help increase Canada's commitment to basic human development.

['Mr. Speaker, like my predecessors, I am committed to supporting francophone or anglophone minority communities so that they can have access to better education, community and school management services.\nAs far as this particular project is concerned, it happens to be in line with our policy to help communities obtain access to better education.\nIn this respect, I can inform the hon. member that the project will be looked at favourably, and together with the community and the province of Alberta I hope to be able to contribute towards supporting this project.']

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister for International Trade once again confirmed that the government intends to proceed very quickly with the bill to ratify the free trade agre-ment between Canada, the United States and Mexico. Yesterday in Washington, however, U.S. trade representative Mickey Kantor stated firmly that the Clinton administration would not proceed with ratification of the treaty until it gets side agreements on labour, the environment and import surges.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he agrees it would be far more sensible for Canada to wait until these parallel negotiations have taken place before proceeding with a bill as important as this one.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say that we believe the North American free trade agreement is good for Canada without having the side agreements on the environment and on labour.
I should remind my hon. friend that in February last year we initiated discussions with the Americans and the Mexicans on side agreements on labour and the environment. They were rejected at the time so we welcome this opportunity to continue the agenda that we commenced in February of last year.
The processes of legislation in Canada, in the United States and in Mexico are under way right now. It is different in each country but it will conclude at roughly the same time. The heads of government of each of the three countries have said that they were committed to the January 1 start-up date. They are committed to not reopening the North American free trade agreement that was signed last December.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the minister that the Americans have decided that they will not proceed unless there are agreements in relation to the environment, labour standards and import surges.
Why is the government not proceeding with its own list, namely a definition of subsidy and a definition of dumping? This week the C. D. Howe Institute said it was a big problem that we did not have clear definitions.
Why does the government not take the occasion to find the solution that Canada needs before getting into that big deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me remind my hon. friend that if we move to a definition of subsidy and changes to the anti-dumping rules we would be reopening the North American free trade agreement.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Each of the three heads of government is committed to not doing that.
My hon. friend cannot have it both ways. If he wants to reopen the North American free trade agreement he has to give something to get, and the Americans want a change in the cultural exemption and a change in the supply management protection. Some members of Congress want to have a change in the dispute settlement system.
Which of those things would my hon. friend like to give to the Americans to get his changes in the dumping and subsidy rules?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not understand in a business such as this one not having a definition of subsidy or a definition of dumping before we get into an agreement. We are having so much difficulty because we have to follow the wishes of the American Congress. When will this government stand up for Canadian interests?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has not answered my question. What is he prepared to give up? He says he is going to open-

March 10, 1993
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
My hon. friend cannot have it both ways. He says he wants to reopen the agreement but he is not prepared to say what he is going to give up.
Is he going to give up the cultural exemption? Is he going to give up protection for the supply management sector? Is he going to give up the dispute settlement mechanism?
Canadians understand that my hon. friend is trying to bridge the differences between the protectionist parts of his party from Winnipeg and the free trade parts of his party from Etobicoke. Everybody sees through that.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of trade knows perfectly well that the United States is imposing new conditions on the North American free trade agreement through the device of parallel accords.
Let me ask a question of the Minister of the Environment. Last November the minister issued a statement in which he announced that the North American free trade agreement "adequately safeguards the environment". Yet only a few days ago in this House the Minister for Science conceded "we have finally got the Americans to talk about such things as environmental protection".
What exactly is this government's position? Does the government still claim that NAFTA itself, the NAFTA text, adequately safeguards the environment? Or, is it now admitting belatedly that the agreement falls short on environmental protection and needs to be supplemented by a parallel accord? Which is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
I thought the question was put to me.
I am delighted to answer a question from the free trader from Etobicoke North. He asks about the provisions in the North American free trade agreement as they relate to the environment. These provisions are as strong as any trade agreement in the world today in the protection of the environment, and I am happy to discuss this at length.
He is asking if we are prepared to have discussions to improve on that. Certainly we are. That was the proposal I put forward back in February last year. We reiterated that in September.
One of the results of this is the North American Commission on the Environment. We have been working with the previous administration and the new administration on the mandate of that. The focus of that will be primarily on enforcement and helping the Mexicans in principle to improve their enforcement capabilities.
My colleague, the Minister of the Environment, will tell us that we have provided, I believe it is, $1 million to help the Mexicans with their enforcement measures. That is the direction in which we are going. It is one of the key objectives of the side agreement on the environment.

Mr. Speaker, let me understand the minister. He says that his objective is some sort of commission on the environment to be created in a parallel accord on the free trade agreement.
Let me ask the minister this question. The United States trade representative yesterday said the United States would walk away from the table, walk away from the agreement, unless it got its three parallel accords.
The minister will know that there is in environment matters, to take one example, a demand on the U.S. part for a trilateral commission which can challenge national environmental law and standards-and that is why I directed my earlier question to the Minister of the Environment-and, second, would impose a broadly based import duty to supplement funding for environmental protection.
Does Canada support that type of proposal? Are we advocating that there be imposed what is in effect a new tariff in what is supposedly a tariff-free zone? Is that the sort of thing Canada wants? Or, has Canada any objectives at all in the negotiation of these parallel accords? What are Canada's objectives?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International IVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will just quote from Mr. Kantor's testimony yesterday as it related to environmental matters. He said: "There is no enforcement mechanism. We are looking at certain national, not supemational mechanisms under the present NAFTA that might be available
March 10, 1993

Oral Questions
in connection with the commissions". There is no intent on their part or on our part to impose our views on standards because that would be an incursion into Mexican sovereignty and that works both ways, as Ambassador Kantor said in his testimony yesterday as well.
We are trying to use this North American Commission on the Environment to raise the awareness, the understanding of how enforcement measures could be used more effectively. That is a major advancement we can have as a result of the North American free trade agreement, because without the agreement we would not be having these discussions at all.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
According to newspaper reports today sources including from the Department of National Defence and other industry experts have raised considerable questions about the attack helicopters that are being proposed for $5.8 billion by this government.
Before the last election the Prime Minister and his government were proposing attack nuclear submarines. Those were cancelled. Will the Prime Minister do the right thing again and cancel these attack helicopters which are not necessary either?

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to glance at the newspaper article to which my friend refers. The article is false.
Parenthetically I tell my hon. friend, perhaps just for the record and I know that she probably will not follow it, these are not attack helicopters. These are helicopters recommended by the military of Canada for search and rescue, for the preservation and protection of Canadian sovereignty, for the fisheries, plus of course to help us in peacekeeping initiatives around the world. They are not for attack purposes. They are there to modernize Canada's fleet in respect of our international obligations.
Let me make it very clear that this government plans to honour all those international obligations.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
I am sure the Prime Minister knows that there is not another country that is purchasing these helicopters for search and rescue, that in fact they are used as anti-submarine helicopters.
I want to say to the Prime Minister who expressed concern for Canada carrying out its search and rescue obligations that we know now the Labrador has had some very serious safety concerns raised by both those who fly that particular helicopter and their families. Clearly if the purchase of the new helicopters is to replace these it will take at least five years.
Will the Prime Minister say today that instead of purchasing $5.8 billion worth of new helicopters, he will refurbish the Labradors, he will do it now and he will think of the safety of those people now, not five years from now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is possible to refurbish the Labrador helicopters at a cost of $1 billion. It would probably extend their life maybe five or ten years. The problem, even if that money was spent, is that it would not bring them up to the search and rescue capabilities of the EH-101.
I share with the hon. leader of the NDP a concern about our aging Labrador helicopter fleet. It is why I agree with the recommendation made by the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs that the helicopters should not only be replaced but it should be done as quickly as possible to avoid costly interim measures. When these new helicopters are delivered we will have the finest search and rescue capability possible in the world. The best technology for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
For a purchase price of $5.8 billion, it seems to me we could have a national child care program, we could deal with poverty in this society and we could have the best country in the world if we chose our priorities right.

March 10, 1993
Oral Questions
I want to ask the Prime Minister, will he do the right thing now and withdraw the purchase of these helicopters in the interest of the programs that Canadians need?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend said in her prefatory remark that there is not another country that uses these advanced helicopters. She is quite right. They have not been manufactured yet.
That is the reason they are so useful to Canadian forces for instances ranging from search and rescue to helping peacekeeping initiatives off the coast of Africa. They are multi-faceted, they are very much needed in the minds of the military to enable Canadian soldiers to fulfil our international obligations.
My hon. friend raises a very good question. Are there other things that we could do with the money? Yes there are. As a government we have tried to constrain the cost of government. We have tried to constrain the cost of growth in government. The problem is not that we are black-hearted accountants but that the cost of servicing the debt is absorbing a greater and greater amount of eveiy tax dollar, thereby diminishing our capacity if I may say to do certain things like the very important matter raised by my hon. friend.
We have established good credentials I think as a countiy in social policy. It is not perfect, but good, and we have established very admirable credentials as a country in defence and foreign policy.
It is the view of the government that these helicopters are required to enhance and ensure the maintenance of that very reputation of Canada for reliability and service to the international community. We have made those decisions, we have established those priorities and we intend to honour them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
Yesterday in reference to an accident involving a Canadian forces helicopter in the Gulf of Mexico, the minister stated that the crash occurred with the Sea King because of old, unsafe helicopters.
Is the minister saying the Canadian forces fleet of Sea King helicopters that our people are flying is unsafe?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, nor did I say that the reason for the crash was because the helicopter was old.
It is in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No. What I said was that it is an aged fleet of helicopters. That is why the hon. member who asked the question was part of a unanimous consensus in the standing committee of this House that the Sea King helicopters be replaced by the EH-101 as soon as possible and I agree with that member.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister who is displaying a frightful ignorance of the matters for which she is responsible.
The quotation yesterday was: "I am aware that the men and women serving in the Canadian forces need to be safe and not made to fly old unsafe helicopters".
The minister knows that the Canadian forces do not have their men and women fly in unsafe helicopters. She should also know that the squadron commander involved in this case stated that it was unlikely that the crash was related to maintenance.
I want to ask the minister why she is playing politics with this important and very sensitive issue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I am playing politics, I am a real piker in that department I assure you.
I am quite prepared to agree with the hon. member that the crash was not a result of maintenance simply because we maintain our helicopters to the highest standards.
The reason why that hon. member and his colleagues on the standing committee voted to replace the Sea King helicopters as soon as possible to avoid costly interim measures-this is the exact wording of the recommendation-is because they recognized that even with the best maintenance in the world, at a certain age those helicopters will not be safe for Canadian men and women. That is why we are replacing them with the finest helicopters and the best technology that we can provide for our forces.
March 10, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence who has not confirmed that the Sea King helicopter is indeed a safe helicopter for our military crews to fly.
The minister knows that the U.S. navy and marines have retrofitted 239 Labrador helicopters. The job is complete. They have retrofitted over 250 Sea King equivalent helicopters. The job is complete. She knows that only Canada among NATO nations has chosen to spend $6 billion of taxpayers' money at a time when the Minister of Finance promises a tough new budget for reasons that are completely inexplicable.
I want to ask the Minister of National Defence the following question. Does she believe the search and rescue helicopter which is now in service, the Labrador, to be a safe helicopter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Labrador helicopter is a wonderful helicopter. Those who fly it are very fond of it.
Have you ever been on it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I have been on a Labrador helicopter. What I would say to the hon. member is that the American Labrador helicopter fleet is younger than our helicopter fleet. When our Labrador helicopters were the same age as the American helicopter fleet, we also did a complete refit of them.
However we are now looking to replace our Labrador helicopters because after a certain number of years there is a limit to what one can accomplish by a refit. Those helicopters are aging, the air frames are too old and it is time to think in advance of replacing them so that by the time they become unserviceable we will have replacements for them.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
I would like to know if the minister is aware that on February 9 three members of this caucus and four members of our staff were told by the senior officers of the minister's department that both the Labrador and the Sea King with a retrofit can fly at least until the year

2020 for one-third the cost of purchasing the EH-101. Why is she not acting on that recommendation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to have the name and the precise detail because that is not in fact correct. Perhaps if they are only flying 500 off the ground and they are not doing very serious missions that may be true.
However our helicopters have very serious tasks to do, both in their shipboard and their search and rescue capabilities. I believe that Canadians need the technology of the 1990s, not the technology of the 1950s, to serve those tasks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. It concerns the issue of the NAFTA and parallel accords.
The Prime Minister said ironically but not surprisingly to an American audience that these parallel accords have little if anything to do with Canada. This certainly contradicts the words of the trade minister.
Yesterday U.S. trade representative Mickey Kantor said: "I am prepared to walk away from the table if we cannot get satisfactory agreements". When asked, the minister responsible said negotiations start next week. We know the American position. It is a strong one. We do not know what Canada's position is.
If the minister is not prepared to defend Canadian workers and Canada's environment, why he is going to the table at all?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend refers to a quote where I said they had little if anything to do with Canada.
He should keep reading the rest of the quote. Perhaps when he rises to ask his next question, he could give the rest of the quote where I indicated that the concerns of the United States are principally with the environment and labour laws in Mexico.

March 10, 1993
Oral Questions
If there are discussions of any kind because of the trilateral and tripartite nature of our fundamental agreement, Canada will be part and parcel of all those discussions to protect Canadian interests at all times.
With regard to the suggestion that Mickey Kantor might want to walk away from the table, good for him. Simon Reisman walked away from the table in 1987 and we got a very good deal as a result of Ambassador Reisman's exits.
Mr. Speaker, some would dispute how good that deal was.
Including Simon Reisman.

Including Simon Reisman. The Prime Minister was quoted as saying that we do not have trans-boundary issues between Canada and the U.S.
Is the Prime Minister aware that there are 43 toxic hot spots in the Great Lakes alone, 30 of them on the U.S. side. Where is the confidence of the Canadian people when these types of people are negotiating our interests?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is a recognition of some hot spots around the Great Lakes, it is because through the Great Lakes action plan and the water quality agreement that we have with the United States, we have entered into agreements with the United States to undertake a clean-up of these hot spots.
In fact there are remedial action plans such as the very successful one in Hamilton throughout the Great Lakes. I may add that we are dealing very effectively with these issues and that the American and the Canadian governments have made the Great Lakes a high priority.
I am happy to report to the hon. member that in my conversation with Carol Browner, the new EPA administrator, I indicated to her that the government wanted to maintain the Great Lakes as a high priority issue between both governments.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of employment.
His deputy minister has admitted that because of the proposed changes to the UI program, new security measures will be imposed at UI offices across the country.
If the government believes that the changes to UI are fair, why does the government need to take new security measures against violence? To what does the minister attribute the anticipated rise in violence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in all fairness to the deputy and what he stated, I think he should be quoted correctly in this House.
What he indicated is that the department is concerned about the security of public servants throughout the country. In recent years we have witnessed in different offices across Canada some acts that are unacceptable. In order to protect our people, we had to have security measures.
We are reviewing on an ongoing basis the security measures in our offices to protect our employees and we will continue to do that.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question for the same minister.
It is obvious to me and to all Canadians that the relationship between the unemployed of this country and this government is deteriorating to the point that new security measures must be imposed in order for dialogue to occur.
Instead of wasting so much political energy on attacking the unemployed, why does the minister not attack unemployment and put Canadians back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the record is clear.
The Liberal Party is still arguing that a person in Canada who chooses deliberately, voluntarily and without provocation to quit a job should be paid benefits.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its abandonment
of aboriginal families and children.
She said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the motion today to focus on what I consider to be the government's dismal record of dealing with the continuing problems that plague aboriginal children and their families. It makes the future of many First Nations people bleaker .
It is extremely sad and deceptive of this government to wear two completely different hats in its dealings with aboriginal peoples. On one hand, the government continues to speak out to the international community in support of the Year of Indigenous Peoples. In fact,

March 10,1993
Supply
Canada is seen to be one of the world's leading supporters and promoters of this event. Yet here in Canada this government continues to do everything in its power to diminish the cultural and linguistic rights and existence of aboriginal peoples.
More seriously, this government continues to let the aboriginal people of Canada teeter on the brink of socio-economic destruction. In many aboriginal communities we have a 90 per cent unemployment and an 85 per cent drop-out rate. We have the highest rates of recidivism. We still have a high rate of infant mortality. We have cancer and respiratory ailment rates that are many times the national average in the aboriginal communities. We also have the cutback of aboriginal economic development programs by 28.8 per cent, which will have a devastating impact on these communities.
This year's theme is Indigenous People's-A New Partnership. How can this government morally continue such a political and international charade? It seems to me that this government has no intention whatsoever to deal with the continuing problems that plague aboriginal communities across this country.
There are many Davis Inlets in this country of Canada. How then can the government expect Canadians, aboriginal and non-aboriginal, to believe that in this Year of Indigenous Peoples "new partnerships" will be fostered when the government's record on the state of aboriginal affairs from coast to coast to coast is absolutely shameful?
Clearly this government has completely lost touch with its responsibilities to aboriginal peoples when the finance minister's December 2 economic statement is a perfect example of this. The government's priorities are clear. Moneys will be spent on other priorities such as the obsolete use of helicopters. Their original purpose for a mission is now obsolete. Cruise missile testing will continue in the north although it is no longer warranted.
Aboriginal interest groups, friendship centres and communications organizations have been hit with 10 per cent funding cuts despite the growing need for these social and cultural resources.
I guess there have to be some shining lights in all this bad news. I attended the Dene Family Symposium in Fort Smith two days ago. It is very encouraging to see first hand the Dene people's focus on wellness. Most important is that the Dene people are doing it for themselves.
In the western Arctic, wellness think-tanks are springing up all over my riding. The community of Fort McPherson recently began an initiative called Pathways to Healing. Another community that is not in the Northwest Territories is sharing its expertise. That is the community of Tadoule Lake which has essentially picked itself up and dusted itself off through wellness initiatives and activities by its own people to return to a more productive community. These efforts allow aboriginal people to come together and pool their ideas at a time when alcoholism and other forms of abuse are rampant in our communities.
I believe that no one has the potential to do for aboriginal people what they can do for themselves. The problem is that in order to help themselves aboriginal people need the funding support of the federal government like all other citizens do to help themselves.
What they do not need are more studies. Communities and people know when they have a problem and what to do about that the problem and what healing is needed. This government needs to act-not listen. Funding cuts to desperately needed and already under-funded programs is not the action that needs to be taken.
I have an example that is very sad. As a result of the recent funding cuts the whole Western Arctic Native Communications Society is in jeopardy of going under. The story is the same around the country. The Press Independent, an outstanding newspaper with a readership of 5,700 and which serves the communities in the western Arctic, had its funding completely cut by the Secretary of State in 1990. The efforts to make it a commercial venture have been very difficult.
As one well knows, commercial ventures have suffered grievously over the last number of years. Numerous businesses have gone under and the bankruptcy rates are very high. To expect a small newspaper of this size to survive on its own is just unrealistic at this time and place.
March 10, 1993

The award-winning newspaper may be putting out its last publication this week. The timing of these difficult cuts at year's end could not come at a more difficult time. While the Press Independent struggles to keep its printers working, book drives have begun in western Arctic communities to satisfy the public's need for more reading materials.
Who tells the story better than newspapers like the Press Independent and Windspeakerl Who tells the story better than those newspapers about the importance of aboriginal priorities, values and traditions? Who puts the pictures out there of our elders and our children and issues that are pertinent to the survival of our people? What tells the story better of the importance of education, of the importance of housing, of the importance of land claims and of the importance of aboriginal rights questions than these newspapers?
There are other areas that are undergoing similar cuts. The National Association of Friendship Centres had a rally this afternoon on Parliament Hill at which a number of members of Parliament have spoken and the leaders of the national friendship centres have appeared themselves.
I have been overwhelmed with letters and faxes as have many members of Parliament, as well as the Prime Minister's office and cabinet ministers' offices I am sure. There were faxes from presidents, employees and aboriginal Canadians who run, work and use the unique services and many resources available through friendship centres and native organizations. From every corner of this country their message is clear to Ottawa. These cuts are unfair and unnecessary. Friendship centres across Canada have closed their doors today in staging a national day of protest.
As I have stated, I spoke at a rally this afternoon. People can best tell their stories themselves and we listened to what they had to say. The Tree of Peace Friendship Centre in Yellowknife is one example of the diversity of resources that friendship centres offer at the community level.
Tree of Peace offers kindergarten programs, adult education, native outreach programs and summer camp programs for children that are very important for singleparent families. It also offers drug and alcohol abuse counselling. All of these services and resources provide
Supply
the means to develop self-esteem, personal development, cultural preservation and community awareness.
Ingamo Hall in Inuvik, Northwest Territories, will have to start charging user fees for its free programs when their $24,000 federal funding cut comes into effect next month. Can one imagine how heart breaking it is for a community that is known for its generosity to charge user fees to its own people for a service it used to offer free?
Many of the programs offered have become the backbone of this community: teen and elder programs, teen drop-in programs, elder social programs and voluntary programs for mothers. These are just to name a few of the programs that are offered by the friendship centres. There are many, many other centres across the country that deserve praise and they cannot all be named. In all ridings of members of Parliament and in senators' communities there are friendship centres that offer an invaluable service that cannot be measured by the government and have a price tag put on it. What can be offered is continuing support and not more cuts.
Another area that is feeling the pinch because of the government's inactivity is the fur industry defence program. I am hoping that the government will come forward and make a firm commitment. Funding for this program has only been committed to the end of this month, March 31, 1993.
We have checked on this and this is the case clearly as of today. At this very moment there has been no money set aside for the International Organization for Standardization or to continue trap research. The Minister of the Environment has publicly stated that there will be no money in place by the end of the month.
It is critical that the environment and international trade departments and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development come up with this money and come up with a cohesive strategy that makes some sense and that offers some hope to the 85,000 trappers across this country.
The economic livelihood of indigenous peoples is being seriously jeopardized by callous and insensitive and mostly foreign-financed animal rights campaigns. We have not heard a peep in terms of strategy from the federal government on how to respond to these groups that are financed to the tune of $20 million. We cannot

March 10, 1993
Supply
as small communities put up the battle on our own. We need the help of the government.
The fur trade industry built Canada and brought the free-market economy to this country. What new partnerships is this government prepared to make with Canadian hunters and trappers to ensure that they meet the European Community requirements in 1995 and allow this economic and sustainable development to continue?
The incomes of 100,000 Canadians depend on access to fur markets. All of these programs enable aboriginal people to make the adjustment and transition from the simple, traditional way of life to the more complex and difficult challenge of integrating into the world of technology.
There is another area. I guess I have talked about friendship centres and also about native broadcast and communications societies that let native people regain their self-confidence and get in touch with their cultural identities through promotion, education and preservation. These are well worth preserving, but there are actually institutes that have been developed by aboriginal people themselves that are undergoing funding cuts. The Dene Cultural Institute in Hay River, Northwest Territories, is one fine example.
It received $200,000 a year from the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs. That is projected to undergo a 10 to 30 per cent cut. This is a cut that will have a direct impact on the future of this institute. Funding cuts will impact this organization's abilities. The Dene Cultural Institute, as small as it is, is a world leader in research efforts to preserve and develop the use of traditional knowledge and the environment and the important need to preserve powerful oral traditions and the knowledge of elders. This does not even mention the work that gets done in the area of sustainable development, conservation and habitat destruction studies and also now in the area of justice program alternatives. Alternative justice programs related to aboriginal communities is something that the Dene Cultural Institute is looking at. A cut as small as this, which to the government may seem harmless, is very much a huge impact on that particular institute and the people who work there.
My hat has to go off to the executive directors of those programs. It has become a very personal mission for
those people to stay afloat and to keep the spirits of their personnel high. For people like Joanne Bamaby who has headed up the institute and has worked for years to develop the programs it is disheartening.
Obviously the government does not see the national and international importance of these resources, nor does it see the importance to provide these services. It is making it difficult for these services to continue. New partnerships in 1993 will not develop without the needed funding. Aboriginal peoples have lost faith in this government in these areas.
Aboriginal peoples have lost faith in the actions of the government with good reason. For example, health and welfare announced a plan to launch the Brighter Futures children's initiative. This initiative is in theory only. It does not seem to exist when it actually comes right down to the funding being provided.
The program was announced almost one year ago, in May 1992. However, today funding still has not been made available. Worth-while programs and desperately needed children's centres remain on hold or must be abandoned.
It is a shameful example of the government's smoke and mirror tactics in dealing with aboriginal peoples and specifically children in this case. We have a particular centre in my riding that could use the money. It wanted to fill out the application forms in order to get the money. It has been working on funding for one year and the Brighter Futures program will offer it not even a hope until the end of April.
It is simply an understatement to say that the plight of the aboriginal housing situation is critically serious. The Government of Canada cannot deny that the Third World housing conditions many aboriginal Canadians live in impact on aboriginal families, their children and their quality of life. The standing committee identified the critical need for housing both on and off reserves in the 1990 report Unfinished Business.
I want to talk specifically about the north because I have a very special mission. I know my hon. colleague for Kenora-Rainy River will deal with this issue in more detail.
March 10, 1993

Other than federal housing, there is virtually no private housing market in the Northwest Territories. Ninety-eight per cent of social housing clients in the north are aboriginals. After months of trying to get the federal minister responsible for housing to reinstate the Northwest Territories housing budget to the 1991 levels, the minister denied this request in September 1992.
Reinstatement of 1991 levels was recommended by the standing committee in its recent report. This federal reduction means that at least 200 fewer cost-shared housing units will be built in the Northwest Territories in 1993. Two hundred fewer. Without reinstatement to 1991 levels the Northwest Territories will only build 153 units across the whole Northwest Territories instead of 372 units.
The need in the north is that 3,945 units are required. There is a huge gap between what the government is able, willing and capable of doing and what it is actually doing or committed to doing, I should say. Without reinstatement to the 1991 levels, the Northwest Territories will only build 153 units.
As you all know, in the Northwest Territories we do not have a private market available to us. We do not have the options available to us as they do in the south. In the past, the Northwest Territories has had a 6.55 per cent protected reserve of national housing allocations. With the projected cuts to the Northwest Territories housing budget, it is now obvious the gap in the shortage of units will never be bridged and will only get wider and wider.
We are all panicking. The minister for housing from the Northwest Territories is extremely concerned about the results and the impact of this reserve not being protected any more and that it will be reduced. This will be reduced and the reason that we have had this reserve is because the need is so much greater and the alternatives and the options are much fewer. It is substantively justified that we maintain this reserve. I appeal to the government not to change this protective reserve.
This shortage in housing has resulted in much higher rates of sexual abuse, family violence, alcohol and drug abuse, suicides and high school drop-outs. The rates are much higher than are found in the south and many
Supply
would say are directly related and linked to the overcrowding in the housing situation that exists.
How does the federal government justify its current spending priorities when northern Canadians do not have the fundamental necessity of adequate shelter to protect themselves from one of the world's harshest climates?
The housing crisis is affecting aboriginal families and children right across this country. Government restrictions on housing funding are forcing bands to build smaller houses and are forcing larger families and their children to sleep in overcrowded basements risking safety.
The basic amount allowed per housing unit needs to reflect the increase in cost of contracts and materials to accommodate the increased cost of the national building code standards.
Bands across the country are put into the position of having to pick and choose the most desperate family in need of housing in the community because the federal housing allowances are not even closely reflecting the actual needs of most bands.
Another issue that is extremely important is post-secondary education. On November 29, 1991 the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development appeared before the standing committee. He stated that the self-fulfilment of the aspirations and the destiny for aboriginal persons in this country required many things including opportunity and encouragement but that education was the most important ingredient of all.
It is unfortunate that the minister could not keep his commitment. The area of post-secondary education is seriously underfunded. The shortage in funding and the waiting list is so great that students have stopped applying to post-secondary institutions.
If you can believe it, in some areas we have an 85 per cent drop-out rate. That drop-out rate allows very few of our students to make it through high school. How then can you justify denying aboriginal students the right when they are eligible to enter college and university?
I appeal to the government. Please, for our children and for our country we need the help. We need the resources in a number of areas that are very serious and

We recently completed a study dealing with housing to which the hon. member made reference. When we were welcomed in her community of Fort Norman we were not greeted in the normal way opposition members would greet one another. Instead, she met us and gave us all a hug. It was a significant bonding process that I experienced in Fort Norman. We took that with us throughout the completion of the study. I want to commend her for welcoming us into the human family as she did. All too often in the things we do in this building we have a tendency to lose our perspective on the real issues. As a result I think the committee operates in a much more productive way.
The minister of Indian affairs at a meeting held with Chief Roland Crowe in whose presence I happened to be did discuss some of the problems that are confronting some of the aboriginal communities. This particular one was the delivery of child and family services.
I believe that from the meeting's perspective, Saskatchewan and the minister seemed to be heading closer to a resolve of the provision of these services. To point to a statistic, in 1991 DIAND funded 36 Indian child and family agencies covering some 212 bands.
There is some progress being made in this progression toward Indian self-government, one that I support quite intently.
There was as well a comment made with respect to education and the fact that there was a drastic shortage in terms of educational funding being provided to our aboriginal children. The number of elementary and
secondaiy students attending band-operated schools has tripled from 13,133 in 1981-82 to 40,513 in 1990-91. During the same period in 1990-91, the number of band-operated schools almost doubled from 159 to 312.
I do not think it is a secret that some of the communities we visited seemed to suggest that perhaps viability might be a question that should be addressed. Some of them were not experiencing the same kinds of services and facilities some southern communities were experiencing. Also, there seemed to be a great emphasis toward the need for further self-government.
Could the member comment about whether or not there are other solutions than simply sending money? I do not mean that in a degrading sense. Other than just making more money available, are there other solutions that we should be pursuing rather than just simply writing cheques?

Madam Speaker, I was very generous and gracious with my hugs because I thought maybe we were going to be given some nice cheques to do a lot of good work.
I know that committees are masters of their own destinies. I have to say the aboriginal affairs committee, many members of which will be speaking today, is a very hard-working and sincere group. What happens in this case is it brings to mind a comment that was made to me by the minister of housing for the Northwest Territories who said: "We can talk about self-government, but if people do not have roofs over their heads, we are talking about a concept without reality". That is very pertinent.
We have to deal with real issues. Health, education, training, child care, housing and land issues are real issues that require resources. There is not a non-aboriginal community in this country that goes unaided from the federal government. I cannot think of one community.
March 10, 1993

It is unreasonable to assume that it is an either/or situation. Every community that wants to build an infrastructure and wants to build a firm base needs the assistance of government. I do not think it goes without gratitude and it goes without the best intent to build the best and the healthiest of communities for all people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to my hon. colleague from Western Arctic. As a member from Quebec, I share her feeling to a large extent. I think that there is a fundamental problem with what is called the Indian Act. Personally, I see that legislation as racist, because it treats a whole culture, a whole people as second-class citizens. So I think that the problem before us today is fundamental. This kind of legislation means that thousands of bureaucrats are used to spend this money, so that there is much less left for the very ones who really need it. I remember asking this question on the Beau-doin-Dobbie committee, where some suggestions to improve the Constitution were made. I asked whether this Indian Act was not rather a program for giving employment to white people, white bureaucrats. It tends to drain off the available funds. Instead of going to the native people, it goes to bureaucrats in Ottawa.
That is the problem with the law now in force. I would really like to ask the hon. member if it would not be better to abolish the Indian Act outright. It would be a big step towards recognizing native rights, because since 1985, I believe, the Government of Quebec has confirmed the right of native people to govern themselves. I would really like to know whether abolishing the Indian Act would not be a big step forward for helping native people set up their own government funds.

Madam Speaker, I am glad that my hon. colleague, whom I have worked with, has asked that question. He had a prime opportunity to support aboriginal people, which would have allowed us to abolish the Indian Act, and that was the Charlottetown accord. This accord would have allowed us to remove the Indian Act.
Supply
The Charlottetown accord would have allowed us to replace the existing Indian Act structure with the inherent right to self-government. This was an opportunity that was lost. I supported this opportunity. I am not criticizing people, I am just saying that it was an opportunity that was lost. It was a prime opportunity where we could have built something and we could have added on to it. Once that opportunity was lost we no longer have that step to take forward at this point that was there at the time.
Sure we can abolish the Indian Act. I am sure, as are my colleagues across the floor. My hon. colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East and the minister have stated numerous times that we have looked for alternatives. The main alternative that we had looked at was the inherent right to self-government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the opposition motion this afternoon. Perhaps I should point out that the amount set aside annually to help aboriginal people has doubled since 1984. We have doubled the amounts spent by the federal government on aboriginal people, and I think it is important to make this clear at the beginning of my speech. Furthermore, in 1993, the department's budget as a whole increased by nearly $300 million.
That being said, today I would like to review with hon. members what I would call the considerable progress made by the aboriginal peoples and the federal government, in a spirit of co-operation, to improve living conditions on Indian reserves. Many of us already know that improving conditions on reserves is one of the four pillars of our government's program for aboriginal peoples.
Hon. members will recall that a little over two years ago, the Prime Minister announced an action plan that would recognize and preserve the special status of the First Nations in this country. This program confirms Canada's commitment to establishing a new relationship with aboriginal peoples. The program supports aboriginal people in their efforts to bring about changes in their communities that will benefit their families and children.

March 10, 1993
Supply
Since the program was announced, hundreds of initiatives have been launched and have had a very positive impact on the lives of members of the First Nations.
Our commitment to improving the social conditions of aboriginal families and children is reflected in the construction of new schools and new housing-for instance in my own region, a new school was opened last summer in Obedjiwan-social agencies offering a wide range of benefits, and assistance in building water and sewer systems. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been earmarked for aboriginal communities from coast to coast to improve living conditions and opportunities for aboriginal people and their children's prospects for the future.
I think we can say that Canadians realize that more must be done to guarantee that future, but I think it is encouraging to see that native health has improved considerably in recent years. These changes are due both to better access to quality health services and to increased community involvement in education and the provision of health services.
If I may, I shall give a brief overview of initiatives that were started in co-operation with aboriginal people. First of all, the health and water initiative which involves accelerating the provision of safe water and water treatment services on reserves. As you know, Madam Speaker, these new water supply and distribution facilities are vitally important to aboriginal communities. Once these facilities have been upgraded, they will not only protect the health and well-being of residents of the various communities but also preserve the environment. Many reserves are located in natural sites where human activity can have a negative impact on the surrounding land and animal habitat. Waste treatment facilities are essential to prevent pollution and disease. Furthermore, this initiative promotes economic development by making the region more attractive to tourists, investors and local industry. The water and sewage treatment initiative is a concrete example of sustainable development.
Substantial progress has also been made in improving housing standards in many Indian communities. The government realizes that the quality and the quantity of
housing on reserves are still a problem and that certain steps must be taken to correct the situation. Nevertheless, the House will appreciate the progress made in recent years in this important field. In co-operation with Indian communities and their leaders, the government has worked very hard to reverse the deterioration of housing on reserves and give Indian bands direct control over their housing programs. It is now up to the bands to decide what is best for their families and children, and the department is helping the First Nations obtain adequate housing by subsidizing housing construction and renovation on the reserves. Government assistance is necessary because of problems caused by legal restrictions in the Indian Act and the limited economic resources of many Indian communities.
Annually, the department allocates nearly $136 million to the housing subsidy program. Over the past 10 years, the Canadian government has supported the construction of more than 30,000 new housing units across the country. The Government of Canada also supports the construction of housing units on reserves by guaranteeing loans. So far the department has guaranteed more than $750 million in loans for housing.
It is clear these are tangible benefits for families living on reserves across this country. The government spends more than $300 million annually to support, either directly or indirectly, housing construction, maintenance and repairs on the reserves.
This spending has clearly had a very positive impact. Nearly 30 per cent of the houses on reserves were built in the last six years, and another 35 per cent were renovated in the same period. Today, almost 95 per cent of these houses have electricity and it is estimated that about 80 per cent of the houses have adequate water and sewage facilities. For comparison, in 1965 less than half the houses on reserves in Canada had electricity and only 17 per cent had an adequate water supply, so we see that there has been real progress on this score.
Again, the government recognizes, I think, that even more must be done to solve the housing problem. We must talk not only about money but about a whole series of things for solving the housing problem. Together with
March 10, 1993

Supply
the leaders, we are working on developing real, lasting solutions to deal with these various questions.
In another vein, we were just talking about education. In our opinion, the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program is an investment in the future of native youth. Federal spending on it has not doubled but tripled since 1984. Federal spending on post-secondary education will be about $1.1 billion over five years. I think that is a more than reasonable amount. The government's philosophy is to help education because it is the way to a more prosperous future for this country.
Speaking of native youth, I think that we must also deal with the more serious situation affecting many communities, which is the high suicide rate, particularly among young people, and situations like the one in Davis Inlet or Big Cove must be addressed. I think that it can be said with certainty that we are doing so and doing it in co-operation with the First Nations and the provincial governments, which is important. We will continue to do what is necessary to develop long-term, not short-term, solutions for improving the quality of life and living conditions in the various native communities throughout the country.
I think that we must look closely at the many initiatives which have been taken with government funding to help solve the suicide problem. These initiatives are part of the total package addressing the mental health of native youth. The Canadian government gives $54 million a year for the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program. Again, I think that we must be aware of the efforts made by the government to help all native communities across the country. Thke Davis Inlet, for example, and let me point out the work of the member for St. John's East who was mandated by the government to work on solving the immediate problems and also to handle the issues connected with relocating this community.
As the minister of Indian affairs said in this House, we approve and support the relocation of the inhabitants of Davis Inlet and the work on this must be done with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and Chief Katie Rich and her council, both for the interim measures and immediate needs and for the development of a comprehensive long-term plan for the community.
Furthermore, immediate action was taken to treat the young victims of this abuse caused by their problems and in the longer term, we will see to it that these young people no longer have this kind of problem. In Big Cove, the government has done the same thing so that what we have seen, heard and read on this subject will never happen again.
It is important to be aware of these realities and of the importance the government attaches to it, both in monetary terms and in terms of the work done by the minister of Indian affairs, or by yours truly in Quebec, with the different communities for the welfare of native people throughout the country and the relations between natives and non-natives and also the relations between native people and the federal and provincial governments.
I think-and I have said so several times since I was appointed to this position-that it is essential to work as a team on this. Whatever the native issue-health, education, land, et cetera-I think it is essential to work as a team. In this regard, I would like to point out the excellent exchange this afternoon between a Liberal member and a member of my own caucus who work together on the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs. I think that such co-operation is essential in the approach that this government wants to take to solve the problems in the community and in the various communities across the country.
There is also the problem of family violence. Again, the government and the department have acted on it. In a four-year period, a little over $36 million will be spent in order to solve the problem of family violence in the various communities.
Each Indian community must determine its priorities. The government, the department of Indian affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare must be there to provide money, yes, but also to help each community according to its priorities and its needs. The more we do as a team, the more positive results we will see. Thke this year, 1993, for example, when 78 per cent of the money will be spent directly by the First Nations. I think this is a very positive indication of the progress that has been made on native issues since 1984.

March 10, 1993
Supply
Nevertheless, much remains to be done, but I think that we are on the way to solving the problems. We would have liked them to be solved yesterday, but they will be solved today or tomorrow. In any case, these problems are being solved and steady progress is being made. This is important for native people throughout Canada because they have things to say to the federal government and they also have their own work to do, just as the federal government has its work to do. With such an attitude, I think that a tremendous amount can be done to achieve our objectives.
In closing, I would just like to remind the House that the motion being considered today does not quite reflect reality, unfortunately, I think. Considering the amounts of money and the work being done by the government and the minister of Indian affairs right now, great strides have been made and we will continue to work with this philosophy in mind-with the co-operation of the opposition, I hope.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the new minister's speech as it relates to a very important issue, which is what is going on in the country called Canada and how this government and past governments have dealt with aboriginal people.
After listening to the minister's comments one would think that there are not a lot of grave difficulties in the country, things are moving and progressing very well, and aboriginal people should be very happy.
I would like to remind the minister opposite, who is fairly new at the job, that on Tuesday, September 25, 1990 we had a very similar discussion in this House when we dealt with the issue of the crisis at Oka. The discussions we had at that time dealt quite extensively with the same things we are talking about today. There are tremendous problems out there and the government has missed all the signals.
I want to remind the minister what the signals are, just so he will know, and then I want to ask him a very specific question, which as the minister responsible he can easily deal with first hand.
The crisis is happening before the minister's eyes. In Davis Inlet six youths attempted to take their own lives;
at Big Cove there were nine suicides in as many weeks; and in my riding, in the Treaty Nine Nishnawbe-Aski Nation territory there have been six youth suicides since the end of December, one as young as 11 years old.
This is not the first time I have stood up in this House and mentioned this problem. So the minister can put this in perspective, since 1988, when I was elected, more than 60 youths and young adults have taken their lives and another 800 have attempted suicide and failed in my riding alone. These numbers reflect that the suicide rate in our part of the country is seven times the national average.
If the minister can stand in his place and say that we are really making progress then he has not been in the same communities that I have.
I want to put a very specific question to the new minister. My understanding is that two weeks ago the minister met with the grand chief from Kanesatake. Two weeks ago he was asked a very specific question and to this date has not given an answer, as far as I know, to the request by the grand chief. In 1990, after the Oka crisis, the committee that I belonged to at the time, the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, was asked by the people to look at the proposal for healing called Breaking All Barriers. Tb this day that healing program in Kanesatake has not taken place.
I would like to ask the minister if he would tell me why. This is a very small request in the over-all crisis that we are dealing with for a community like Oka, which went through probably one of the most severe situations that any community would ever want to face in this country or any country in the world. It had the army come in on them and was put in a situation where for generations the scars will be visible to everyone, as we talked about that night.
Now is the opportunity for the minister to do a very small thing, and that is to accept the recommendation of that community for the necessity for a healing program and put it in place.
