speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. minister who has just spoken on this matter before us today. The minister may be aware that I rose in Question Period a short while ago to ask about economic development funding scheduled for aboriginal communities.
The chief of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations, Chief Roland Crowe, wrote to the Prime Minister on February 10 expressing concern about potential cuts to economic development programs as a result of the finance minister's mini budget on December 2. At that time Chief Crowe indicated that the Saskatchewan Indian nations had done a study of what potential cutbacks would mean. He said they would devastate the emerging First Nations economies, create bankruptcies in Indian commercial and industrial fields, result in the countless loss of existing jobs and damage the future of their communities and their memberships. They acknowledged that they are the most disadvantaged and deprived group in the country. Chief Crowe put this on the record on February 10.
Last week the government issued the 1993-94 estimates and confirmed that this government has cut back funds for economic development to the Indian bands for 1993-94. I quote from the estimates that we have from the other day. Economic development is on page 14-7 of the estimates: 1992-93 estimates were $54 million and for 1993-94 the figure is $33 million.
We see the government removing the tools necessary for growth in the aboriginal communities, some $21 million in the coming fiscal year.
I would like to ask the minister how at a time when Indian people require economic development to ensure the futures of their communities the government can justify the removal of money from the economic development portfolio.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate although it is not a debate that we want to see happen in this House over and over again, as has happened. I should remind the House what the motion is. It states:
That this House condemns the government for its abandonment of aboriginal families and children.
As one of my colleagues from the Liberal Party pointed out just a few minutes ago, this is not the first time we have dealt with this kind of motion in the House.
As I said before, we deal with it over and over again. It does not really seem to matter which government is in office, whether it is the party opposite or the party to my right, this same motion seems to come up on the floor over and over again. At some point, the people in this House have to take seriously what they are debating and take a serious look at the information that is being placed before them.
I congratulate my colleague from Nunatsiaq for bringing this motion forward. I congratulate my colleague from Western Arctic and the minister for being involved in the debate. It is an extremely important debate.
It was precipitated, as members know, by a number of stories in the media recently that have placed a stain on Canada's reputation as a promoter and supporter of human rights, both nationally and internationally.
The incident at Davis Inlet a few weeks ago was mentioned earlier, where a number of children barricaded themselves in an unheated building with gasoline and other materials, including inhalants to sniff, hoping that they would inhale enough of this material and it

March 10, 1993
Supply
would become cold enough that they would kill themselves and not have to face the morning.
What kind of a country is this that Canadian children feel they are forced to do this kind of thing? They are children being forced to commit suicide so that they will not have to live through the terror of the following days.
Members will recall that in the same community the same kind of thing had happened over a year ago. Again children found themselves in an unheated house. Forced to heat the house, they created a dangerous fire situation and burned to death. This was in the same community a year previously.
What kind of people in a country like Canada are forced to the kind of despair where they are willing to bum themselves to death? They really did not care whether they burned themselves to death because it was better to them than facing the terror of the next day.
The same thing has happened, as my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River pointed out, in the area around Big Trout Lake in the Nishnawbe-Aski area of northern Ontario where there have been 800 suicides attempts since he took office in 1988. Eight hundred Canadians, most of them very young, most of them teenagers, attempted to take their own lives rather than face the terror of the following days.
How would you feel if you were a parent of one of those children and you tried to tell them there was a better future for them? Would you feel comfortable taking the minister's comments that we have actually added a few more million dollars to the departmental budget of the department of Indian affairs and that that is going to prevent these children from doing that kind of thing? According to the minister, they will not have to do that any more because the government has added a few million bucks to the department of Indian affairs. Certainly that holds no promise for these children.
At Big Cove in New Brunswick, we heard the same thing. I watched parents interviewed over and over on television being asked about the suicide epidemic. The elders in the community were being asked about the suicide epidemic. They felt almost like a kind of tidal wave, that their own children were doing it and they were powerless to stop it. They do not know which
buttons to push. They do not know which arguments to make. They do not know what is going to be affected. Their children simply do not want to live through the terror of the coming days.
There are not many of us in Parliament today, but we in Parliament have been given an opportunity-and again I would like to congratulate the two members who put forward this motion-to take this issue of the suicide of adults, young children and teenagers in aboriginal communities seriously.
It is unfortunate the way the motion is worded but on opposition days that is the way you have to word motions. It means that the government has to vote against it, the opposition has to vote for it and as a result nothing comes of it. If only there was a sense on the part of the people in this House that they really wanted to deal with the issue through a motion like this and that the three parties could get together with the independents and get something going that will stop what is happening in aboriginal communities.
As I said, this is a stain on our reputation internationally. I am astounded at the reaction the government has to the incidents that took place at Davis Inlet, at Big Cove, at Big Trout Lake and in other communities around the country. It sends the deputy minister around on a tour of Europe on essentially a mission of denial, telling people that Indians actually have a great life here in Canada and not to pay any attention to those isolated incidents at Davis Inlet, at Big Th)ut Lake and Big Cove. They are told to ignore those incidents because that is not the real Canada.
It is a process of denial that we should not be involved in because aboriginal children in this country have the highest rate of suicide in the world. It is not just seven times the rate of other children nationally or other teenagers or other populations nationally, aboriginal people in Canada have the highest rate of suicide in the world. There are reasons for this and we should be looking at those reasons.
Instead of one party attacking the other party attacking the third party over their failure to deal with aboriginal children and families, we should actually be developing
March 10, 1993

solutions and motions that all three parties can vote for so that we can get something done on this issue.
The minister's response is that the government has increased spending by a few million dollars. Nobody believes it. My colleague from Western Arctic pointed out the series of budget cuts that have taken place recently. A lot of those budget cuts have been done on the backs of aboriginal people.
What has been cut? Aboriginal friendship centres that serve a tremendously valuable purpose to people who have left their reserves in the country, have come into the cities and need the kinds of services that are provided by friendship centres in order to survive in what they see as a culturally hostile surrounding. important issue that affects the reputation of this country internationally.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
It is hard not to get angry on this issue when, as I said, hundreds of aboriginal teenagers are dying and nobody seems to give it that much attention. That is the whole point of this resolution and the whole point of the member presenting it. I certainly salute those motives and those intentions.
I listened carefully to the minister's response. It is a response that we seem to get all the time when we bring these questions before the House of Commons. The government seems to have this response. In fact it developed the response through an organization that developed a program called Special Words and lactics.
The government found out through its studies that Canadians were concerned about what was happening to aboriginal people. They were concerned about the high levels of unemployment in aboriginal communities. They were concerned about the high levels of poor health and about the survival of aboriginal children. They were concerned about the high rates of violence in aboriginal communities.
Canadians are sympathetic. They demand that their government deal with those problems. The government says how much money is being spent on aboriginal
communities. In order to develop the figure, it uses every stamp licked to send pension cheques to retired Department of Indian and Northern Affairs public servants. It pads that bill to about $4 billion, almost the cost of the helicopter program. It pads the figure unmercifully to show Canadians that it is spending a tremendous amount of money, but in fact it is not and the evidence for that is the rate of suicide among aboriginal kids.
I am a member of the aboriginal affairs committee of this House. Members of that committee work well together because we take a problem solving approach. We have travelled to many of the aboriginal communities around the country and we have seen the problems firsthand.
It does not matter whether members are from the Liberal Party, the Conservative Party or other party members who attend the committee. Once they have seen the problem they know they have to start developing solutions for them. They know solutions cannot be developed unless they enter into a process of consultation with the people involved who are better able to solve their own problems provided they have the resources. Then solutions can be worked out.
I suppose that is what I was hoping would come out of the resolution, but I gather from the minister's response to the resolution that the government intends to vote against it. I really do not see how it could do otherwise.
We did a study on aboriginal housing. We listened to the people from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development tell us that of the 70,000 on-reserve housing units in this country, 35,000 of them are unliveable, as Indian Affairs staff described. Half the housing units used by aboriginal people on reserve are being described by the department responsible for them as unliveable, and 60,000 more units are needed to bring housing standards for aboriginal people up to the same level other Canadians enjoy.
The cost of that program would be in the order of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. That is not a great amount when we compare it to the cost of the helicopter program. When we look at the damage being done to Indian families and to aboriginal children as a result of the housing problems we cannot afford not to spend that money.
March 10, 1993

I said it would take $2 billion to $3 billion but that $2 billion or $3 billion, if it were spent in the right way, would generate a tremendous amount of employment in aboriginal communities building the infrastructure, the sewer and water systems, the roads, the foundations and the houses. All this effort, all this work, could provide employment for aboriginal people currently unemployed and drawing welfare. It would draw down the deficit of the country and make those citizens producing, contributing citizens again. They want to do it. It is just that the government has not taken its place in the partnership and has not provided the resources.
We found that bad housing causes a lot of problems when we visited those communities where housing is a problem. It causes problems such as alcoholism, abuse, domestic violence and sex abuse. It causes problems with education. All those problems related to housing cost the country millions of dollars. We could deal with the problems by reducing the amount of overcrowding in housing and making good quality housing available to aboriginal people.
I will wind up by saying that it is a good resolution. The government should pay attention to it. We are not providing enough resources and the government has the resources. The helicopter program has shown that. Why does not the government respond to this situation and do what should be done rather than hark back to the amount of money it is currently spending, which clearly is not enough or we would not see the symptoms we are seeing in aboriginal communities?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to my colleague with whom I have sat for a number of years on the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs. He will know that since we have been involved on the same committee there have been discussions and studies dealing with housing.
The issue in a nutshell is simply that since 1983 we have been in the process of studying a housing policy for aboriginal people. Later when I have an opportunity to speak I will give the numbers of the backlog and the percentage of those who do not have sewer and water. We could go on and on about how grave the issue is.

Could my colleague give us some indication from his perspective of why it is that the government, knowing the particular backlog and knowing how overcrowding can affect the lives of young people, cause mental stress and anxiety in these communities and result in the suicides we talked about, would not come forward with a comprehensive policy program to deal with the very real problem of a tremendous lack of good housing in First Nations communities?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is an excellent question. One of the reasons the aboriginal affairs committee dealt with the housing issue in the first place was that the member lobbied the committee because of the concerns he had for housing in his riding and in northern Ontario. It is a major issue.
It is surprising that the government does not deal with this issue. The government says that it wants to get the economy of Canada going again. It wants to get us out of the recession. It wants perhaps to focus its programs on some of the poorest of poor Canadians so that they can begin to lift themselves out of the recession. It wants to do away with and reduce the amount of welfare end unemployment insurance it is paying.
Here is a clear opportunity for the government to do that. It could start rebuilding the aboriginal housing stock and providing some of the 60,000 new units needed to accommodate the growing aboriginal population. It would create tens of thousands of jobs, as I pointed out. It would restore hope in aboriginal communities. It would get people away from the kind of desperate life-style that drives them toward substance abuse as we have seen in Davis Inlet.
This is the kind of thing the government should be doing to bring Canada out of the recession. In addition it would bring the welfare charges down, as I pointed out before.
This has all the elements of something a government should be doing to cure the problem of the recession. Why do government members not do it? I suspect it is because they are Tories. They do not really feel that the government's role is to get involved in the economy that way. As a result, it is ideology that is preventing them from doing something that would be valuable for the Indian people, valuable for the country and valuable for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the member knows, I was one of the members on the aboriginal housing committee who made a number of recommendations to government. The report of that committee was a unanimous report and I stand by the recommendations made in it.
The problem with this issue is that the government, as I said in my speech, has to make the resources available. I know the member is familiar with the contents of the report, but I think what is needed in this case is the money and that is $2 billion to $3 billion to provide that kind of housing. than to allow the department of Indian affairs to acquire housing for them on a low-bid system outside aboriginal communities.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am extremely pleased to be given the opportunity to address this particular topic today.
It would seem to me that what we need to do is to highlight one flagrant contradiction. The government, it seems to me, without exaggerating the discussion that has just preceded, is in fact speaking with a forked tongue. The government is speaking internationally about aboriginal rights and the importance of the aboriginal year. Yet, at the same time, there are serious cuts that are being undertaken to aboriginal programs. I will give those in some detail shortly.
What we have to recognize is that the aboriginal people are really suffering a double or triple hit because they have an extremely unique and distinct situation in our society that I would like to explore with my colleagues and with Canadians who are listening.
Let us look at the government's record on education. When we do that let us remember that we are talking about all Canadians and that includes in a number of instances many aboriginal Canadians that are being affected. If we look at EPF reductions, cuts in transfers for health and education, from the government in Ottawa to the provinces and territories, we will find that roughly $30 billion will have been cut in the course of a decade. It is about $20 billion for health and about $10 billion for education.
It is important to recognize that it is not only all Canadians, but within that particular group our aboriginals are also being hit. Look at training and retraining. There are a lot of debates about increases in funds. There are increases in funds but it is Canadians who are paying those funds to the government to use for training and retraining. It is not from the general revenues. Look at the need, at inflation and at what was promised Canadians in terms of the best training programs in the
Supply
world. We should recognize that not only all do Canadians need more training to bring them up to date, make them more productive and make them more competitive, but aboriginals are also involved there. They are being hit here as well.
Look at research and development. The government promised to double its investments in research and development. We know that it slipped dramatically. It is not even close to what it had hoped. In fact, it has slipped from what it was. It was 1.40 of Gross Domestic Product and I think it is around 1.20 right now while our major competitors are at 2.80. That affects our aboriginal communities. Within the area of research and development is the whole field of social sciences that looks at questions of abuse, poverty and many other social challenges that this nation faces.
Of course we recognize that our aboriginal peoples are affected in a very dramatic way by some of the social difficulties that Canada is experiencing as a whole. Any reduction in over-all funding will affect them too.
Look at illiteracy for example and the number of functionally illiterate Canadians. We recognize that there is a disproportionate number of aboriginal people. Yet there was a reduction in the most recent government estimates on investments in literacy. Therefore, our aboriginal peoples are being affected negatively over all.
Let us look more specifically at aboriginal people per se. We know the plight of native Canadians. We can argue all we want whether or not the government has been fair or unfair. I do not think that is the issue. The issue is how much is needed to correct the situation. What is it that we need to do to make sure that they get the same opportunities that the rest of Canadians do? That is the question that we need to be addressing. Look at the unemployment rate, for example. It is high. It is in excess of 11 per cent. There are over 1.6 million Canadians unemployed. However, if we look at aboriginal peoples per se, we find that they are hit dramatically. Look at social assistance. There are over two million Canadians who are on social assistance. Look at the number of aboriginal peoples who need social assistance and compare their numbers as a proportion of the whole. Look at illness and suicide and other measures such as that. We find that our aboriginal people do not compare favourably at all.

March 10, 1993
Supply
If we look at housing there is an awful situation. It is extremely disappointing. Look at the drop-out rates in elementary and secondary schools and at the number of graduates in colleges and universities and then compare that to the whole population. We find that they do not compare favourably.
I maintain that it is not their fault. I maintain that a series of governments over the years, perhaps well intentioned, have not been able to make the progress they should have made. What we need is more assistance. What we need is a renewed commitment. What we need is a recognition of the problems. What we need is to stop arguing about whether we increased it or decreased it. What we need is to put forth the resources that are required in order to permit aboriginal people to compare favourably with their Canadian counterparts who are their Canadian brothers and sisters.
Look at post-secondary education specifically. You would know, Madam Speaker, that there has been a cap placed on it. Of course, that has been increased somewhat and I do not want to get into that argument. However, let us remember that there are more aboriginal peoples today who want to go on to post-secondary education. Obviously it needs to be increased.
We have new legislation that permits members who were otherwise outside of the aboriginal community now to get into the aboriginal community. The ranks have swelled. Look at the cost of education over the last few years. Those costs have skyrocketed so any kind of cap, whether it be minimal or otherwise, needs to be increased substantially under those circumstances.
I want to share with my colleagues here in the spirit of openness and debate some of my concerns. I have a memorandum and I just want to raise a couple of frustrations that have been shared with me. I quote from this particular memorandum from MMC in Ottawa: "To date there have been no self-government agreements concluded with Metis people". There is a great sense of frustration.
I want to share with you the sense of frustration that our aboriginal peoples have had when $21 million has been cut from economic development for Indian Affairs. Economic development provides education, jobs, training and learning. There was a further cut of $6 million from the aboriginal economic strategy by ISTC. There
again was a major blow or hit suffered by our aboriginal peoples.
Why was 10 per cent cut from the native friendship centres?

We know these friendship centres not only welcome the people from these communities who come to our cities but also provide all kinds of support, including apprenticeship programs.

One million dollars have been taken away from the Northern Native Access Program.

Why? This was a very successful program that gave our aboriginal people access to some very important positions.

Why has government reduced funding to aboriginal political organizations? I know that they can be somewhat difficult on governments no matter what governments they are, but surely this is a problem. There is the Arctic Environment Strategy, which is a program that affects our aboriginal people. Why has this been cut by $2 million?
Here is the basic question. I do not want to raise the question of helicopters again, but I do want to raise the question of priorities. These are important dollar cuts to these small groups of people that are not being given the same opportunities. Look at large expenditures in relation to those smaller expenditures. Canadians and aboriginals are asking why this is happening.
I simply say that I do not think it is people-

-who are knowingly intent on doing the wrong thing. I think they just do not have their priorities straight.

It was a year ago today that this House honoured Louis Riel. I shall terminate with a quote from my address on that particular day. I am sharing my time with my colleague the member for Kenora-Rainy River. I want to leave perhaps on a note of some optimism. Last week in Manitoba there were two important historical events. A Metis was named Lieutenant-Governor of Manitoba. Hopefully that appointment will permit our aboriginal
March 10, 1993

peoples to re-energize, to go forward and to realize some of their goals that have been long outstanding.
Last week in the province of Manitoba, the Supreme Court decision with respect to the government and French language schools was also important. It has implications-

-for Francophones across Canada, and I imagine for Anglophones in Quebec as well. But I think it could also have implications for our aboriginal people.

If francophones and anglophones can manage their school systems, as I think they should-

-why not aboriginal people?

It would be a great step forward if somehow we could empower them to take over their education and training and retraining opportunities for their peoples.

I want to conclude with the following quote: [English]
In the spirit of justice, and at a time of great instability in this country, I urge the House to take one more step to recognize Louis Riel not only as a founder of the province of Manitoba but also as one of the Fathers of Confederation. A year ago we made that statement.
I am hoping that these gestures, along with political will, will permit us to go forward.

tion. We discussed education for those groups in which he is particularly interested, the francophone communities of Manitoba and Ontario, as well as the aboriginal communities of Ontario and Manitoba and others across the country.

Of the money that we spend, 77 per cent is spent by band councils.
In band-operated schools the number of students has increased from 13,000 to 40,000 over the past 10 years. Thirty per cent of the teachers in band schools today are Indian teachers. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's comments and the statistics he shared with us. I do not challenge them, because I did not have a chance to look at them.

As I indicated before, the debate should not be so much about how much the increase or decrease has been. Decreases are serious in any programs because our aboriginal peoples have so many needs.
If I, for example, were to take a decrease in salary of $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000, it would not be nearly as serious as if I were earning $12,000 or $13,000 a year. That is the issue that we are debating today. Of course there will never be enough money for all of the things that we want to do for our society, I appreciate that. However, at the same time we must continue to strive to remedy that which is wrong. This is definitely wrong.
I know my colleague well enough to know that he shares a belief in the direction in which I want to go. That is, to respond to actual need to the extent that we can and to try to avoid cuts affecting those small groups who depend very much on that kind of support and whose only real opportunity to get out of the cycle of poverty and some of the social difficulties they are encountering is through education, training, retraining, and economic development.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to enter this debate by making a similar suggestion to the members opposite as I did many months ago in September 1990 when we discussed this same kind of situation as it related to another crisis that was at hand, which was the crisis of Oka.
At that time I said to the people across the way that it is important that they listen before the crisis takes place. The problem we are facing again today is the same problem we faced in 1990. It is that the government goes through the motions and pretends to be listening to what Canadians and members of Parliament opposite are saying, but in fact it is not.
I am going to put some things on the record and would be very pleased if anyone would wish to dispute them and get into the argument.
The government has abandoned aboriginal families and children by ignoring the socio-economic issues after the failure of the Charlottetown accord. It has washed its hands of all aboriginal issues, resulting in families and children being ignored. Examples of that, and there are many more, include Davis Inlet where six youths attempted to take their own lives and Big Cove where there have been nine suicides in as many weeks.
In the area where I come from in northern Ontario, which is Nishnawbe-Aski Nation territory, there were six youth suicides since the end of December, one as young as 11 years of age. Since 1988, and this is something that I have raised on many occasions, there have been more than 60 youths and young adults who have taken their lives and, this is something which the people across the way sometimes tend not to focus on, there have been 800 other suicide attempts that have failed.
We do not have to ask ourselves why on this side of the House. We know why. Aboriginal youth in northern Ontario feel a sense of abandonment by their governments. The suicide rate in Canada among aboriginal peoples is seven times the national average. We have to ask ourselves why.
I will explain why. It is because this government has failed to implement a mental health policy for aboriginal peoples. That is why. It is not that we have to do more studying. It is not that we need to consult any more. The time for consultation and study is over. It is now time for action. We need a mental health program in this country.
Wellness does not only include physical well-being. It is absolutely essential that a national aboriginal mental health policy with programs aimed at dealing with suicide and the crisis in aboriginal communities be implemented immediately. We do not need any more studies, we need action.
Let us look at some of the root causes of aboriginal suicides. As has been mentioned in this House today, there is a housing crisis in aboriginal communities. We all know that overcrowding in aboriginal homes is 16 times the national average. Half of on-reserve housing is inadequate and unsuitable for living in. Those numbers are well known.
We as a standing committee, as I have mentioned before in this place, and other members across the way have studied the issue on behalf of aboriginal people. We know what the numbers are. We know what the statistics
March 10, 1993

are. It is now time for the government to come out with a policy to deal with this situation.
As a result of this kind of situation aboriginal youth have no privacy for studying and no space they can call their own. They are surrounded by too many people in these small houses.
Has the government moved to address the on-reserve housing crisis? No. The funding levels for housing, as I mentioned to the Minister for International Trade, have not increased since 1983. Family violence is an offshoot of overcrowding, the lack of funding for education, and the lack of a mental health program.
Aboriginal youths are finding it impossible to deal with violence that they live with on a day-to-day basis. Many see committing suicide as the only way to escape that violence.
Another issue is the economic development situation. This government likes to talk about the importance of economic development for the future of Canadian citizens, and of course aboriginal people are a big portion of that.
On June 12, 1989 in Calgary, the minister of state for small businesses announced the creation of the Canadian aboriginal economic development strategy, known as CAEDS. The minister remarked that: "Even in this day of expenditure restraint the federal government has demonstrated the importance it attaches to aboriginal economic development by maintaining and indeed somewhat increasing the level of resources that it will devote in this area. As important as the amount of money so allocated is to the Government of Canada, it has decided to commit itself to long-term support for aboriginal economic development. Unlike previous programs that had sunset dates this money will form part of the government's base budget and will not have to be renegotiated every five years".
As we all know in this place, that is a false statement as of this date. We all know that the Main Estimates for 1993-94 tell another story. Funding to economic development has been cut for this year from $69 million to $48.7 million, a reduction of 28.8 per cent.
Supply
What we can read into that whole process is that we would rather pay welfare than stimulate economic development and get aboriginal people back to work. Welfare payments to aboriginal people also come from the public purse so if we want to continue to pay welfare payments in this country then we will continue to do what the federal government has done in its estimates, which is cut the tools that will give people the ability to have jobs and create jobs for their own people.
The unemployment rate in aboriginal communities in my riding stands at over 60 per cent in some cases and is as high as 80 per cent in others.
Aboriginal youths have very little opportunity to find jobs on reserves. Now that economic development funding has been cut their chances of finding a job are almost nil.
Aboriginal youths feel a sense of despair. They have lost hope in their future. They see no way out of the cycle of poverty and dependency. They see a government that does not give a hoot. They feel abandoned. They take what they see as the only avenue left, which is to take their own lives.
This is a national tragedy and an international disgrace. We are supposed to be a caring and compassionate society, but instead our national government has abandoned aboriginal families and children.
It is unfortunate that we on this side of the House have to come forward with a condemnation of the government's record on aboriginal issues and suggest an opposition motion which would say to people in Canada that we as parliamentarians in the federal government have done a disservice to our people and their future by not taking this issue as seriously as we should.
We have also done something else. We continue to not listen to people when we are told as parliamentarians that a crisis is looming in particular sectors of our society.
As was mentioned before, and I think it is important to put this on the record as it relates to housing, overcrowding in housing is 16 times the national average. The backlog requires 12,000 units to address it. Funding has not been increased since 1983.

March 10, 1993
Supply
If we want to seriously deal with aboriginal youth suicide in this country we are going to have to deal with the causes. The causes of course are the despair that people feel because of the lack of a mental health policy by the Government of Canada and the resources necessary to have good mental health programs. There is the very important issue of a stable environment through a decent place to live without which causes family violence and with that the despair I have been talking about.
I hope we have been able to suggest to government that there is a crisis and that it not continue to bury its head in the sand and say: "Look at all the nice statistics. The budget has been increased in certain areas by 5 per cent, 10 per cent or 12 per cent". When the population is growing on reserve four times higher than the national average, a 37 per cent increase in the last 10 years, these piddling increases to the budget are not going to resolve the difficulties and the crisis in those communities.
If members opposite and the ministers that are responsible want to give aboriginal youth a chance and a decent hope for the future, they have got to get on with the job of creating programs that are effective and that will work.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment to make. The hon. member talked at some length in his remarks about housing.
I have the honour to represent 22 bands in northwest Saskatchewan. Every single one of them has housing as a priority. The report on housing by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs outlined these circumstances quite clearly as a situation affecting aboriginal people in Canada.
I support as strongly as I possibly can the report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs entitled A Time for Action: Aboriginal and Northern Housing. The report indicates that the shortfall in aboriginal housing today is about $3 billion. It is a shortfall that the people living on the reserves within my federal boundaries know all too well exists.
When I visit with the chief and the councillors or when I visit with the band members living on these reserves, I am constantly made aware of the lack of housing available to the individuals living there. I am appalled at
the circumstances that have resulted in large families having to share very small and outdated accommodation.
I am overwhelmed by the lack of ability of the government to respond to those needs, given the political will and the finances that have been made available to the department.
Just this year alone I have had several bands approach me and talk to me about the funding that was available to them at the beginning of the year. They made housing starts during the year only to be told once the basements were dug and the foundations were poured that the department had no more money. Those housing starts would have to be put on hold until the following year. Basements sat throughout the winter months with the snow falling, accumulating and melting in them without the ability of the bands to complete those houses.
I simply want to state that I would like to see the government take immediate steps to correct the deficiencies which exist in the housing program. It would like it to accept and implement the recommendations that are in the report of the standing committee that indicates housing matters must be addressed and must be addressed immediately.

Mr. Speaker, of course it is very important that members get their statements on the record and I appreciate that the member has done that.
I also suggest to the member that one of the major problems with housing as far as aboriginal people are concerned is that the Government of Canada has not, at this moment at least, put forward a policy on housing to deal with the crisis we are talking about. It also has not recognized that housing is classified as a treaty right.
There is one thing that should be put on the record for people who are watching and listening to these speeches today. That is that the dollars given to aboriginal communities for housing are a subsidy. In essence the government tells the aboriginal people that it will give them a certain percentage.
In my region for example, they will be given roughly $27,000 toward a house. We all know a house cannot be built for $27,000. Then the government tells the aboriginal people they can get the rest of the money for that particular program either on the open market by borrowing from the banks or by going through CMHC. Or they
March 10, 1993

can do it another way and that is to take it from their minor capital.
For those who are not aware of what the minor capital money is for, it is normally used to help with infrastructure. For example, it is used for roads, water, sewer, band offices, street lighting. What has happened is that because the minor capital in some communities is so small, the chiefs and councils are forced to have to make tough decisions as to what is more important, the housing that people are asking for or the other infrastructure problems they are facing.
In the 46 reserves that I represent in Kenora-Rainy River, on average we build two to three houses. When there are known backlogs of 50, 60, 70 houses in some of these communities, we are forced to build only two or three at a time.
If the government is serious about dealing with this crisis it will have to first of all recognize housing as an important part of the treaty right and second, put funding toward it.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
A short time ago we were all shocked to learn of native young people sniffing gasoline and the terrible consequences. We know that gasoline in Canada contains various toxic substances, such as toluene and manganese. We know that in the penal systems in the state of California studies show that the most violent offenders have higher levels of manganese in their hair samples.
Is the member aware of any studies conducted in Canada on the impact and consequences of sniffing gasoline containing MMT? Of course MMT is not allowed in the United States.

United States. I thought we should find out what drives young people in this countiy to sniff gasoline. I then went a step further on the advice of my colleague. I went to the United States and asked if any studies had been done on this particular issue. We would also like to go a step further on one of the matters. I suggest to the House that we should as a Parliament and as a government on the other side look at the effects of manganese on young people when it is in their systems. We should determine whether that is the particular substance in gasoline that makes young people high and determine the reasons they use it.
Because my colleague has a private member's bill to ban MMT in gasoline I think we should seriously look at the ramifications of that. That is because sniffing gas is one of the biggest killers in aboriginal communities.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to enter the debate in the House today on this very significant issue and to lay before the House some information that I think is necessary for the public to hear.
Aboriginal programs continue to be one of this government's highest priorities. Between 1984-85 and 1992-93 the total federal expenditure on programs for aboriginal people has grown from $2.6 billion to over $5 billion.

March 10, 1993
Supply
In spite of the current effort to reduce government expenditures, the 1993-94 Main Estimates reflect a further increase of over $351 million in over-all funding to aboriginal people. This represents a 7 per cent increase government-wide.
The government remains committed to implementing with aboriginal people the native agenda that was announced by the Prime Minister in September 1990.
That initiative focuses the government's attention on four fronts. First is the settling of native land claims. Second is to improve the social and economic conditions in aboriginal communities. Third is to build a new relationship between aboriginal people and governments. Fourth is to review the fundamental place and role of aboriginal people in a contemporary Canada. Substantial progress has already been made on all of these pillars of the agenda.
The government's continuing financial commitment is again evident in the 1993-94 Main Estimates. For example, funding for specific claims will grow 74 per cent to $136.5 million. Comprehensive claims funding will grow 24 per cent to $95 million. Funding for elementary and secondary education on reserves will increase by 9 per cent to $745.2 million. Funding for the Inuit and Indian post-secondary education program will grow by 6 per cent to $213.3 million. Social services expenditures will rise by 10.1 per cent to $898.9 million.
In recent years the growth rate of expenditures on aboriginal programs has exceeded the over-all growth of federal expenditures. While the over-all growth in federal expenditures between 1991-92 and 1992-93 was limited to 3.1 per cent, funding for aboriginal programs increased by 7.9 per cent. Even with tighter restraints on federal spending in 1993-94, expenditures on aboriginal programs will still grow by 7 per cent.
Within the department of Indian and northern affairs, four main activities accounted for about half of the estimated 1992-93 expenditures. While most of these activities are akin to those provided to non-aboriginal people by provincial and municipal governments such as elementary and secondary education, social assistance and welfare services, they also include post-secondary education.
Since 1981-82 the total of these four activities has grown at an average annual rate of approximately 12 per cent. Of course expenditure levels are only part of the
story. What aboriginal people are doing with these funds is the real indicator of progress.
This government continues to support the devolution of responsibility for the delivery of services and programs from DIAND to the direct control of First Nations.
A range of innovative funding mechanisms has been developed and introduced to aid in this process. This includes contributions, alternative funding arrangements, flexible transfer payments and grants. By the end of 1991-92, 77.3 per cent of the expenditures of the Indian and Inuit Affairs Program of approximately $2 billion was fully administered by First Nations through band councils, tribal councils or other Indian organizations. This figure has increased by 15.2 per cent since 1985-86 when bands administered 62.1 per cent of Indian and Inuit Affairs Program spending. Indeed, the control is moving to where it belongs, which is to the Indian leaders.
Since 1981-82, federal funding for elementary and secondary education has increased approximately 9 per cent annually from expenditures of $272.9 million in 1981-82 to an estimated expenditure of $683.7 million in
1992-	93 and planned expenditures of $745 million in
1993-	94.
In the process the number of elementary and secondary students has grown from 80,466 students in 1981-82 to 96,594 in 1991-92. The participation rate of on-reserve children aged 4 to 18 in elementary and secondary schools has increased from 87.6 per cent in 1985-86 to
91.4	per cent in 1991.
At the same time, Indian children are staying in school longer. The percentage of children reaching grade 12 or 13 through normal progression has risen from 33.9 per cent in 1985-86 to 47 per cent in 1991. More of these children are being educated by their own people. The number of elementary and secondary students attending band-operated schools has tripled from 13,000 in 1981-82 to 40,513 in 1991. During the same period the number of band-operated schools has almost doubled from 159 in 1981-82 to 312 in 1990-91.
As a result of special post-secondary education programs providing opportunities for Indian students to become qualified teachers, 30 per cent of the teaching staff in bands schools are now Indians. Since 1981-82, federal funding for DIAND's post-secondary education assistance program has increased more than eightfold from an actual expenditure of $25.1 million in 1981-82 to
March 10, 1993

an estimated $201.3 million in 1992-93 and a planned expenditure of $213.3 million in 1993-94. This has more than quadrupled the number of post-secondary students receiving assistance from 5,467 in 1981-82 to an estimated 21,442 in 1991-92.
Indian communities are also improving living conditions with DIAND funding. We have heard comments from earlier speakers about housing. On-reserve housing expenditures, including the construction and maintenance of houses, schools, roads, bridges, sewers and other community facilities have increased 34.2 per cent since 1985-86 from $102.7 million to $137.8 million in 1992-93.
In 1991-92, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development allocated $131.6 million in direct capital subsidies, and $127 million in loan guarantees to housing. Between 1983-84 and 1991-92, an average of 3,212 new homes per year were built on reserves. Just under 4,000 homes per year were renovated during the same period. In 1991-92, about 91 per cent of dwellings on reserves had an adequate water supply compared with slightly over half in 1977-78. The proportion of dwellings with adequate sewage disposal has increased considerably from about 47 per cent in 1977-78 to almost 80 per cent in 1991-92. Electrical service had reached less than half the houses on reserves in 1965. In 1991-92 it reached 88 per cent.
The government also continues to support increased Indian control of development, design and delivery of child and family services. In 1992-93 the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development funded 41 Indian child and family agencies covering 213 bands. Between 1980-81 and 1990-91 the percentage of children in care has decreased from 6 per cent to 4 per cent.
Throughout this period of devolving responsibility for delivering programs and services to First Nations, DIAND itself has been shrinking. The number of authorized person-years in Indian and Inuit affairs programs has decreased 42 per cent from 4,463 in 1982-83 to 2,608 in 1992-93.
The percentage of the budget of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that is di-

rected to administrative overhead has declined steadily through 1980 and the early 1990s.
In 1985-86 the department overhead was 6 per cent of the over-all budget administered by DIAND. In 1993-94 the rate is expected to be 3.2 per cent. Yet the statistics for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development do not tell the whole story of this government's commitment to aboriginal people.
In 1993-94, federal expenditures on aboriginal programs were administered by 12 departments. Of these, 98 per cent came from the following departments: Indian Affairs and Northern Development, some 72.2; Health and welfare Canada, 14.9 per cent; Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, 5.1 per cent; Employment and Immigration Canada, 3.7 per cent; Industry, Science and Technology, 1.3 per cent and Secretary of State, 0.8 per cent.
There are many departments within the federal government working to make conditions better for aboriginal people. This reflects both the diversity of the federal programming for aboriginal people and the many co-operative government-wide programs that benefit their communities.
For example, the quality of health care available for Indians is improving considerably. Between 1976 and 2001, the life expectancy of status Indians is expected to increase by approximately 10 years. Health and Welfare spends more than $735 million annually on programs and services to further this goal, of which approximately 25 per cent is managed by the First Nations people themselves.
In 1992-93, as part of a $136 million federal initiative on family violence, $36 million was provided directly to Indian communities to deal with family violence on reserves, including $22 million from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and $14 million from Health and Welfare Canada.
This represented a fivefold increase in DIAND's share from $4 million in 1988 to $22 million in 1992. Another $160 million will be provided to promote community health and the well-being of Indian families through the aboriginal component of the Brighter Futures strategy.

March 10,1993
Supply
The federal government's commitment to improving the quality of the environment for all Canadians was confirmed when the cabinet approved the green plan in
1991.	The green plan included two programs that are particularly important to aboriginal people: the Arctic Environmental Strategy administered by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Indian Health and Water Initiative, a co-operative initiative administered by DIAND and national health and welfare.
The $92 million Arctic Environmental Strategy is not limited to aboriginal communities, however, since it is dedicated to cleaning up the environment in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories where aboriginal people account for substantial portions of the population, it is of intense interest to them. Indeed, when we were having hearings on the green plan I was fortunate enough to attend the hearings in Yellowknife, Whitehorse and Iqaluit and I had the opportunity to speak with Inuit and Indian people. I know how important the environment in that part of the country is to the Inuit and Indian people.
The Indian Health and Water Initiative was launched in March 1991 as part of both the green plan and the native agenda.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's $250 million share of this program is being used to upgrade water and sewer services on reserves while Health and Welfare's $25 million contribution is helping to improve the quality of drinking water.
Some 125 communities have been identified as priorities for work under this initiative and are already benefiting from the program. Most of them are managing the funds and projects themselves, as it should be.
This government is also committed to closing the gap between the availability of adequate housing for Indian people and the growing need for it. That commitment involves increasing Indian control over the design and management of the program.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and Central Mortgage and Housing are
working together on a new housing policy that will meet this need.
Meanwhile, DIAND's housing program and CMHC's on-reserve housing program have been exempted from the government's current deficit reduction measures.
In 1993-94, expenditures by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development alone will be $137.8 million and will provide for the construction of approximately 3,300 houses and the renovation of an additional 3,200 housing units.
CMHC will continue to provide planned, new on-reserve housing. Nearly 25 per cent of all new moneys under its social housing program, $41 million in 1993-94, will be directed to native people living off reserves.
The Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy that was mentioned in the House earlier, CAEDS as it is called, was launched in June 1989 to provide the means to help aboriginal people manage business enterprises, economic institutions, job training and skill development.
Three government departments are contributing to the five-year program: Employment and Immigration Canada, Indian Affairs and Northern Development and Industry, Science and Technology. By bringing together aboriginal people, governments and the private sector, CAEDS is making a substantial contribution to expanding First Nations' capacity to build their economic future and has considerably enhanced their prospects for success.
The strategy is channelling federal support and assistance to hundreds of new and maturing aboriginal enterprises. This includes everything from gas stations to motels to grocery stores to airlines.
Since its launch there has been tremendous growth in the capacity of aboriginal communities to initiate and manage their own development projects. There are now more than 10,000 Indian businesses both on and off reserves reflecting Indian entrepreneurial activity and participation in the larger economy.
In 1991, DIAND approved 22 direct loans valued at $1.2 million to Indian and Inuit businesses, 46 loan guarantees valued at $3.2 million and 4 fee-for-service contracts and loan portfolio sales totalling $723,000.
March 10, 1993

Industry, Science and Technology Canada, which has the lead responsibility for financing native businesses, provided $72 million.
Training opportunities under CAEDS hold special promise not only for aboriginal people but for Canada as a whole.
Demographic projections clearly demonstrate that Canada will face a severe shortage of skilled labour within the next few decades. With a younger population than non-natives and with increasing opportunities for training and education, aboriginal people are in an exceptional position to play a greater role in Canada's economy.
Pathways to Success, the aboriginal component of Employment and Immigration's Canadian Jobs Strategy, is one such opportunity. It continues to contribute $200 million a year to training and employment initiatives for aboriginal people. Under the pathways program, aboriginal management boards at the national, regional and local levels decide on their training priorities and how available resources can be used best to meet their own people's labour market needs.
The funding for Pathways to Success is part of the $347 million this government will spend on aboriginal economic development in 1993-94. While this represents a reduction of 7 per cent over all from 1992-93 levels, it is still a significant investment in the future of aboriginal people in their communities.
On another front, many First Nations are anticipating future land claim settlements by eagerly exploring joint ventures and business possibilities in mineral development, oil and gas and tourism just to cite a few examples.
In addition to having access to specific aboriginal programs, aboriginal Canadians are also eligible to participate in federal programs for non-aboriginal Canadians. Examples are old age security and unemployment insurance.
Moreover, the Indian Act exempts from taxation the property of an Indian, including income, that is situated on reserve. Where purchases are made on reserve, and in certain other cases, the exemption applies to the goods and services tax as well.
Supply
In spite of the significant gains aboriginal people have made, there is still considerable room for improving their social and economic conditions. The federal government recognizes that aboriginal people are still among the most disadvantaged Canadians generally, and remains committed to helping them overcome this disparity.
I know that all of us here today share one objective: healthy and satisfying self-sufficiency for aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the minister's remarks. I know she has held responsibility for Indian affairs in this country for a couple of years. I know she has been on many reserves throughout the country, therefore this is not a new subject for her.
As I listened to her remarks, I tried to make the linkage to what the percentages were, the dollars were and what was really going on in the reserves. This is what really troubles me about the debate so far today.
I forget who it was who made the statement: Seeing something once is better than reading about it a thousand times. I have been to Iqaluit, Whapmagoostui, James Bay, Oka and other places across the land, like Barriere Lake. What is going on in those places is just not good enough.
I think of Whapmagoostui in the northern part of Quebec where we have an arena structure. The arena beams have been set up for three years and the rink has not been finished. I am not talking about a lot of money here. I think there are a lot of things that could be actioned that would not cost the taxpayers of Canada a lot of money. From time to time when I turn on television and I see the program World Vision I watch the suffering, the lack of facilities, water, sewers, educational facilities of people from disadvantaged countries. We look at all of these

March 10,1993

places from all around the world but the reality is we have conditions in our country that are just as bad as anything we see on World Vision.

I do not agree with the NDP, by the way, that government members do not care about the aboriginal community. I do not believe that. I cannot believe that. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's comments. The 14 months that I spent in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development gave me an opportunity to travel from coast to coast and visit many reserves.
Yes, I have seen exactly the same situations that the hon. member mentioned. I have also seen the growth and commitment of our native people on other reserves as well.
In Tionaga, just down by Belleville, a group there started their own charter company with one plane. Two years later they have nine planes which they bought with their own money and are running a very good charter service.
The Six Nations Reserve, which is close to my own home, has a beautiful new senior citizens and nursing home so that elderly native people can stay on their own reserve and be well cared for.
There are reserves in British Columbia and the Atlantic provinces that are showing this type of growth and development but we still do have areas that need more help.
Where they need the help, and what we have tried to do to get the bureaucratic problem out of the way, is to
devolve responsibility to the native people so that those people that are on their own reserves set their own priorities as to what they want from life on their own reserve. Maybe it is not a hockey rink, maybe they would sooner put the money into housing. In another case they might want the rink because they want their young people to be able to play hockey.
I think the best growth and development and help that we can give the native people is to give them the responsibility, along with the funding, to allow them to move forward and make their own decisions. Not decisions made by us sitting in this House and debating or by the members of DIAND, but rather let them make their own decisions and plan their own future.
This is why education is so important and why I am so pleased to see the growth in post-secondary education. Those young native people are leaving reserves, getting a post-secondary education, coming back and applying that knowledge to the growth and development for their younger brothers and sisters that are on those reserves.
That is where I think we have to concentrate. We have to concentrate on allowing our aboriginal people to make their own decisions, to conduct their own lives, to have the funding but let them make the decisions as to where they should spend it.
It is only by making their own decisions, by making their own commitments that things will begin to happen, so that they will have what they want on their reserves to better their particular way of life. I think that is the move we have to make. The fact that we have devolved the control of some 77 per cent of the spending back to the native people where I think it should have been all along is a step in the right direction. I would like to see more of this continue.
I am very proud of the accomplishments so many of our native people have made. The work they have done under the CAEDS program, the businesses they have gone into, the employment they have created for their own people, speaks very well of their ambitions and their abilities to make a difference in the lives of their own people and I think that is the most important part of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too listened carefully to the minister and I agree with my colleague from Toronto that this is not a question of laying blame on one side of the House. We all share as legislators-they happen to be the government at the moment-some responsibility for what is happening.
I listened to two particular points that the minister made. It seems to me they are key points. One was the issue of education and one was the issue of self-government. What she says makes a lot of sense. Those are the things that had to be emphasized. The unfortunate part of it, as I understand it, is that not only have the funds for post-secondary education been kept but the funds for native communication programs, native broadcasting, have been diminished if not completely eliminated.
Supply
How can people devise their own future? How can people talk among themselves about what should go on if they cannot communicate? We have had native radio and television broadcasting systems that broadcast in Inuit that have been scaled down to the point where they are ineffective. This is key for people, if they are going to talk about their own future they have to talk together in their own language.
In the north we are inundated with signals from the south. We are inundated with sitcoms from American producers. The diminishing of post-secondary education funding and the diminishing of native broadcasting systems needs to be reviewed.
I have a good idea, Mr. Speaker, and maybe I will try it on the minister now. We talk about self-government. Clearly that is a key issue if people are going to make any progress at all. I listened to what the minister said about CAEDS. She told us about certain native groups across the country making progress, developing their private sector and their entrepreneurial skills and their ventures. Some of that is happening.
My colleague talked about James Bay. The Indians in James Bay are a case in point. The symptoms that we see across the country of alcohol abuse and family violence surely point to the fact that by and large our native people are in a desperate situation. Getting control of their own lives, getting an independence, is key for them. Self-government is the key issue for that.
There are still 600 unsettled land claims. The question becomes how and when they are going to be settled. They are still unresolved. There is an Indian Claims Commission which does not have the authority to advance a claim but only to make recommendations to the government and to mediate. Clearly the quick resolution of specific claims is urgent.
What is the policy of the government? We might remind ourselves of the debate about helicopters that has been going on in this House this past week. It is prepared to spend $6 billion for new helicopters. We could argue that they are needed or that they are not needed. I am not arguing whether they are or whether they are not. We on this side happen to think they are not and the government thinks they are.

March 10, 1993
Supply
The point is that to govern is to choose. If we set a priority that this is more important than settling land claims, do we have our priorities straight? We do have a responsibility for the Armed Forces but we have a responsibility to the first people. That should be our first priority. If we are looking at a meagre supply of resources available to the government for doing things that need to be done, surely the land claims settlements of aboriginal people have to be at the top of our list.
I want to get back to symptoms again. Recently a community in my riding was in the news quite a bit, the community of Davis Inlet. I just want to put on record some of the statistics with regard to that community in case the camera lens has now left Davis Inlet and moved to focus on some other part of Canada or on some other part of the world. We happened to be in the range of the camera for a while and that was great, but now the camera lens has moved away.
I want to remind the House and the people of Canada that Davis Inlet is still there. There are 465 people in Davis Inlet, 297 of whom are youths. Of the 297 youths, 42 are habitual sniffers. Of the 42 youths, 14 are chronic sniffers and some may have suffered permanent damage from sniffing. Of the 168 adults, over 100 abuse alcohol. Of the 100 adults, some 31 are chronic alcoholics.
I know the hon. member across the way is doing his best to resolve the situation. I know he is providing leadership on behalf of the Government of Canada in consultation with the Government of Newfoundland to come to grips with this. I know discussions are going on between the two governments and with the community to try to resolve it. In the final analysis it is that community which must make its own decision, must take control of its own life and must plan for its own future. The impetus for the future prosperity and well-being of that community must come from within. I hope it will.
I know the process is in place whereby we can deal with this, but I wanted to put on record some of the statistics we may have forgotten, because that camera lens has deserted us and moved elsewhere.
These are symptomatic. I do not know how my time is going. I want to leave enough time for my colleague from the north who gets a lot of credit for bringing this resolution forward. Let me say again that the symptoms
are conclusive that there are serious problems across the country: a problem in health and a problem in education which must be addressed immediately. We must have the funds to deal with them. We must have a mechanism for speeding up the settlement of land claims. Within that land claims settlement self-government is a key issue, a priority issue, an issue that must be addressed.
We have to put it at the top of our agenda. We cannot say that we are going to deal with it at some time. This is a problem we have as responsible people on both sides of the House. We owe it to first citizens to show them we are prepared to deal with it on an urgent basis.
I compliment my colleague from Nunatsiaq for the motion and for bringing this matter to the attention of the House and to the people of Canada. I hope, as a result of the debate we have had today, progress can be made not simply in Davis Inlet or in Sheshatshits in my riding, not simply in Nain, Makkovik, Hopedale, Rigolet and all along the Labrador coast where we have serious problems that must be addressed, but all across the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to thank my colleague for his remarks and his sensitivity to the issue.
One thing I sometimes try to focus on and to elaborate on as often as I can for members of Parliament who do not represent First Nations communities is the necessity to be much more sensitive to a particular culture that is not the same as their own and to try to put themselves in the shoes of a First Nations person.
In the discussion in the House today, and I want to ask the member to comment on it if he will, it was interesting that the minister who spoke just before him talked about how the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development passed on in the last few years a lot of the responsibility to First Nations to run their own lives, to the tune of close to 70 per cent, if I am not mistaken.
I am concerned that there is a suggestion by the minister in that statement that First Nations have the power now to make the decisions to improve their lot and the way their lives are looked after at the grassroots level or at the community level. My concern is that in
March 10, 1993

fact all we are doing as a government when we make those suggestions is misleading the public.
What we are asking First Nations to do is to administer policies that are within the department, policies that have been made by non-natives. If we want to take it a step further, that suggests to me that chiefs and councils probably have less powers than mayors or reeves in municipalities would have.
Would the member tell me and tell the Canadian people-and he could use Davis Inlet or some such community in his riding as an example-how much power those people have over their own lives to improve their lot, to make a go of the community they so desperately want to improve, and to give young people the future they expect to have?
That is really the essence of this debate. It is not the numbers the minister across the way is throwing at us. The government is suggesting that it is trying to put more money into it. It is the responsibility and ability of First Nations to truly make a difference in their own lives that I think we should deal with in this debate.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on that question. There is a fundamental truth in what the hon. member is saying. I think he is saying that it is power. That involves some resources but maybe not so much resources or certainly not only resources as power. Politics is a question of power.
We understand that there is a federal system whereby power resides in the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments. Everybody quarrels that they do not have enough.
In the communities in my region there is, as the member says, less power to govern those communities than municipalities would have. For example, there is not control over their own schools. There are no native health people in the communities I am talking about.
I have to make a distinction between Inuit communities and Innu communities. The Innu, as the House knows, are Indian people and the Inuit are not. I have to make a distinction between those two types of communities.
Supply
In the Indian communities in my riding there is a clear lack of local control for the institutions and for what could be called the municipal structure. There is a long way to go in creating that but that is what we must aim toward. We must give people control over their own lives. It is not easily done, but it must be done. It is fundamental.
If any of us in this Chamber do not have control over our lives we do not have any self-respect; we do not have any direction; we do not have any identity.
The essential problem is how to give people back their identity. We should give them back control over their own lives. What that means is saying to them: "We do not tell you what to do from Ottawa or St. John's or anywhere else; you decide". As with Moosonee, Moose Factory, Winnipeg, Trois-Rivieres, or any other place in this country, they decide where they want to go as communities. Davis Inlet, Sheshatshits and those other communities have to do the same. They must have that element of self-government.
