speechtext:
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut]

We have proposed this motion today to bring attention to the many unmet needs and aspirations of the aboriginal peoples in Canada.
This year, 1993, is the year the United Nations has designated as International Year of Indigenous People. It is surely appropriate for the House at this time to examine the government's performance on issues of concern to aboriginal people.
On a wide range of issues basic to aboriginal families and children from coast to coast to coast this government has failed to act. Where there has been activity it has been piecemeal, sporadic and ad hoc.
This House and Canadians have to know that behind all the big numbers and fancy rhetoric tossed out by the government, aboriginal peoples and communities throughout the country are in real distress.
Recently the tragic situation at Davis Inlet to which the hon. member who just spoke before me referred shocked Canadians and many other people throughout the world. Under the intense media scrutiny and outrage of ordinary Canadians the government was forced to

March 10, 1993
Supply
take some action. Beyond the government's initial response much more remains to be done. It is more important than ever, now that media attention has abated, for all of us to ensure the government follows through in a fair and just way.
Today I would like to draw attention to the many other aboriginal communities in Canada which are in similar despair. Many of them are remote, far from the political and media centres of Canada. From time to time a story will be written in the newspapers or graphic images will make the television news but this attention is not sustained. I am sure that the government would do much more if only Canadians knew more about the issues confronting aboriginal peoples.
What if there had been massive media attention in the 1950s when several Inuit families were relocated from communities in northern Quebec to the isolation of Resolute Bay on Grise Fiord in the Northwest Territories? What if their suffering and hardship had been chronicled daily for all Canadians to see?
Without that media attention we only have firsthand accounts of the survivors and their descendants. Their words, however, are not good enough for this government. For the past several years the High Arctic exiles, as they call themselves, have documented the circumstances and consequences of this relocation and have tried to obtain an official apology and compensation from the government for the suffering they endured. Having heard their testimony the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs has twice since 1990 asked the government to respond positively to these requests. The government has refused.
The Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples is holding a special inquiry into this issue. Zebedee Nungak, a spokesperson for the exiles, summed up the government's attitude in this way:
They have condemned the exiles to a second exile. The first exile was the relocation itself and the second exile was the government's determined effort to ignore the claims and allegations of these people.
Relocations, loss of land base, loss of traditional economic activity, erosion of language and culture, and loss of control have created tremendous strains and pressures in aboriginal communities. In the most remote communities these pressures are more recent, but recent
or not the consequences are the same. The repeated and continuing impositions and encroachments of non-aboriginal cultures, values and governments on aboriginal peoples have had and are having devastating results. The government has failed once again to recognize these strains and its own role in contributing to them.
The activities of animal rights groups destroyed the sealing economy in the eastern Arctic. Unless the government acts quickly, Canada's European markets for wild fur will be lost and so will the livelihoods of many aboriginal trappers. The government knows that by 1995 Canada has to meet certain international humane trapping standards to keep our European markets. Yet last June the federal cabinet refused to provide any new money to continue on expanding its humane standards development program. Aboriginal trappers are already having a hard time trying to provide for their families and this government is just making it harder.
Throughout the country aboriginal unemployment rates continue to be unacceptably high. It often reaches 70 or 80 per cent or 90 per cent in very remote communities. Aboriginal per capita income levels are well below those of non-aboriginal Canadians.
Aboriginal health conditions have been described by health professionals as Third World conditions. The rates of aboriginal violent death and suicide are many times greater than the average Canadian rates. Aboriginal housing conditions are far below Canadian standards and yet progress on these and many other issues is painfully slow or non-existent.
Study after study has documented inadequate, unsuitable and overcrowded aboriginal housing conditions and a backlog of crisis proportions and yet the government has not acted. In fact it has cut housing funds. The last time any additional housing funds were provided to deal with the housing backlog was in 1983, 10 years ago, under a Liberal government.
This government's refusal to act has made aboriginal and northern housing problems worse. Despite a housing shortage of 3,600 units in the NWT, the federal government reduced its funding for cost-shared social housing. With the full knowledge that current housing construction rates are not keeping up with the expanding northern population, the government instituted cutbacks.
March 10, 1993

The crisis continues, the backlog worsens and the problems increase.
By failing to respond to the north's critical housing needs the government has failed to deal with the quality-of-life issues associated with housing. It has ignored the impact of the lack of available, suitable and affordable housing of all areas of life.
Post-secondary education plans are postponed or not pursued at all due to the lack of housing. If someone has a house they risk losing it to someone on the waiting list if they leave their community to go to college or university. The severe overcrowding creates stresses that contribute to family violence and other social problems. There are homeless people in the Arctic. There are families living in shacks on the edge of Iqaluit and Frobisher Bay and this government has turned a blind eye to their plight.
Last year the federal government turned down a request for more housing funds for the Northwest Territories. Related to family violence and housing is the north's urgent need for more shelters, facilities and services to support victims, offenders and their families. There is also a need for more child care facilities and spaces. This government promised a day care program that never materialized. As a result, northern child care needs are not being met. About 2,300 children in the NWT require child care yet there are only about 700 licensed spaces available.
Health conditions are also related to housing conditions. Tuberculosis is still a problem in the Northwest Territories. Meningitis occurs at higher rates in the Northwest Territories than in any other part of Canada. Deaths among Dene and Inuit babies in the NWT still occur at twice the Canadian rate and the gap between aboriginal and non-aboriginal death rates in early life is increasing.
From 1984 to 1989 in the Northwest Territories over 30 per cent of all deaths were the result of injury and violence. The NWT suicide rate is more than twice the Canadian rate. In the 15 to 24 age group the NWT rates are more than five times the Canadian rate.
Something is terribly wrong. Why are so many aboriginal young people killing themselves? They seem to have no hope and they do not see any prospects of improving their lives. They have no jobs. Aboriginal employment rates are not improving. Aboriginal unemployment is not decreasing. It is getting worse. An unemployment crisis
Supply
threatens the use of the north and yet the government has done absolutely nothing and is doing absolutely nothing.
Between 1986 and the year 2016 the population between the ages of 15 to 64 will increase by 137 per cent in the central and eastern Arctic or Nunavut. The present rate of job creation is hardly sufficient to absorb the growing population. Excluding opportunities that arise through the creation of the Nunavut government, at the current job creation rates fewer aboriginal people will be employed in the year 2016 than were employed in 1986.
Without concerted and dramatic attention to this problem and the need for much greater investment in education and training the aboriginal people of Nunavut will become increasingly unemployed.
Perhaps this government's greatest failure has been its lack of vision, its failure to see the whole and its refusal to listen to the solutions offered by the aboriginal peoples themselves.
All the issues I have touched on are interrelated and interconnected. Aboriginal peoples want these issues addressed urgently and holisticly. They want long-term preventative strategies developed which reflect their priorities and goals. All too often however, the government has provided only short-term reactions when it responds at all.
The aboriginal peoples of Canada have contributed much to the building of this nation and they have much more to offer. While several of them have managed to circumvent the obstacles placed before them, too many others are being lost. This tremendous waste of energy and talent cannot continue.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for his remarks.
Of course as an aboriginal person himself he has a much larger understanding of the issue than any of us in this place. I think something we desperately need is someone who can tell us firsthand just what is happening.
One of the things that I wanted to ask my colleague relates to post-secondary enrolment. Ministers have spoken today and the minister of Indian affairs is going

March 10, 1993
Supply
to speak later this evening in this debate. He could probably help clarify this as well.
The number of aboriginal people enrolled in post-secondary institutions nearly doubled since 1985-86 to 11,170. It ended up in 1991-92 to be 21,442. It is easy to see that there has been almost a doubling of the amount of young people who are interested in and are enrolled in post-secondary education as far as aboriginal people are concerned.
I am interested in asking my colleague this. The ministers opposite continue to say that funding for post-secondary education for aboriginal young people is going up and that it is really improving.
In the capping that took place a few year ago, we found that between 1990-91 and 1991-92 only 142 students more were enrolled than in the previous year. If one looks at the numbers that I gave regarding 1985-86 to 1991-92, a rough estimate shows that there's an increase every year of almost 2,000 students per year going to post-secondary institutions.
We find in a recession that most people tend to go to school because they cannot get a job with times so tough. They go to school to upgrade their skills and training. In fact, only 142 more young people went to school than in the previous year.
That number interests me in that it suggests that the capping has had an effect on young people and their ability to go to post-secondary institutions.
I would like to know from my colleague's perspective from the north whether he is aware of young people who have not been able to go and are on some sort of waiting list because of the effect of the cuts in post-secondary education to aboriginal students.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question.
First of all, one must understand that young people have to want to go for post-secondary education. We should be giving them every opportunity to do that. However the incentive sometimes is not there because they have to move somewhere else where the environment that they are used to is not there.
In the area of post-secondary education in the north that we are talking about, unfortunately the enrolment
rate is not very high. It is partly because of the amount of paperwork that is required to take the step to go into post-secondary education. I have a nephew who wanted to go into post-secondary education yet decided not to at the end because he could not get through the paperwork.
However, I remember when this government wanted to cap the post-secondary education funding. The cry from the aboriginal people across the nation was heard by the Canadian people, yet it took the government so long to respond that at the end only so many took advantage of it as the hon. member just mentioned. They get to a point where they give up because they are not given the incentive. They do not have the faith in this government's ability to react to the issues that they want to get involved in. I think it is time the government realizes that it has an obligation to the aboriginal people of this country and realize that aboriginal people will take over only when they have the post-secondary education needed to take over the kind of jobs they want and the kind of government that they want.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
I am pleased to participate in this debate on a motion sponsored by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq. I am glad that he is in the House to be present for my comments in this very important discussion.
First, I would like to say that I share the member's concern and that of all members, for the condition in which many aboriginal people find themselves in their communities across Canada. For anyone who watches television or reads the news it is evident that there are indeed very sad and even tragic circumstances in some of the aboriginal communities in Canada today. I think we all feel a deep sense of conscience and obligation to do everything within our power to alleviate these conditions.
At this point I depart from the language of the motion before the House where it condemns the government for abandoning aboriginal families and children. I sincerely believe that this government has done more to improve the situation of aboriginal peoples in Canada in the space of the last eight years, and certainly in the last three
March 10, 1993

Supply
years while I have been minister, than has been done since the time of Confederation.
Assume one judges improvement by the level of financial support from government that now exceeds $5 billion a year to status Indian and Inuit peoples. If one multiplied that by all the years that the government has been trying to help through subsidies and welfare in overcoming these problems, one would have to admit that the policies and programs of successive governments of the past have been an abysmal failure. If we still see these tragic scenes on our televisions of any child without a bed in which to sleep, of inadequate conditions, inadequate housing and health problems then one must admit to the failure of policies of many decades.
Therefore, I want to speak today about the successes of the last few years, many of which will not be fully understood and measured until some years into the future. I believe it is important to accept that funds alone and the recognition of rights alone will not solve these fundamental human problems.
Let us set the record straight at the outset.
Within First Nations communities in Canada today, compared to 20 years or 40 years ago, on average all of the statistical indicators show that educational levels are much higher, life expectancy is significantly improved, the level of infant mortality is far lower than it was even 20 years ago, employment levels are higher, and economic development opportunity is greater. I am told there are now 5,000 aboriginal businesses in Canada today, compared to less than 1,000 a decade ago.
Housing quality and standards are much improved. There are new schools. I have visited and opened many of them. There is cleaner water and running water, and there are improved services in most communities and much higher standards of health. I am not saying this to erase the truth about the tragic situations that still exist, but there has indeed been a significant improvement.
It is important to recognize something about the system of paternalism created by our well-meaning ancestors who thought the European ways of raising children, harvesting crops and building communities
were superior to the aboriginal ways, their languages, traditions and form of subsistence. We tried to make them be like us.
We created an Indian Act shortly after Confederation and immediately put First Nations people on to small parcels of land-some called them concentration camps without fences-and told them we would protect them and ensure that their rights and their special relationship to the Crown would always be respected.
In doing so we took away the freedom of aboriginal people to make choices for themselves and gave to a person in Ottawa-I happen to presently be that person-the power under the Indian Act to make all decisions affecting their lands, resources, education, and way of government. That person essentially exercises a veto over any choice they might wish to make about their own destiny.
In retrospect that has been a case of very bad judgment. If we are to continue to see progress in the living conditions and in meeting the needs of young aboriginal children growing up in a modem and rapidly changing world we must end the paternalism that the Indian Act, my ministry and Indian reservations represent.
There are three keys to a brighter future for aboriginal people, who one day we hope will come into a full and complete partnership with all other Canadians, into a true equality. The three keys to getting to that brighter future are education, adequate resources, including land, and self-government. Of those three the one that is of fundamental importance is education.
On coming to this portfolio I discovered that in 1960 less than 4 per cent of all young aboriginal people made it to or through high school. In 1985 that figure had risen to 40 per cent. In 1980 less than 1,500, perhaps 1,000, aboriginal students were getting into post-secondary programs. Now that number is more than 20,000. In 1984 when we formed the government there were approximately 4,000 to 5,000 students in post-secondary programs. Now that number exceeds 20,000.
Education is a fundamental tool for self-reliance and self-determination. At the same time there must be something to do with that education, and while preserv-

March 10, 1993
Supply
mg a traditional way of life it is no longer possible to live on the resources of the land in traditional ways.
The First Nations, the native communities of Canada, are surrounded by forests and have largely survived economically since the encounter with European civilization through the fur trade. It is a strange paradox that the fur-bearing animals are no longer accessible to them nor can they be sold in adequate abundance because of policies and environmental changes.
The forests which we cut down and convert to newsprint and two-by-fours from which we build our homes are largely used and enjoyed by non-aboriginal peoples, even though that is the primary resource that surrounds most First Nations communities.
We need to settle land claims and deal with the question of sharing more equitably in energy resources, mineral resources, forest resources and the power that can be generated from water.
Even if we can settle land claims, honour treaty obligations, provide enough land and resources, and the level of education is adequate we will still not see thriving, successful and self-reliant aboriginal communities without self-government.
In the years ahead that is going to be a fundamental challenge to all the members of this Parliament and those who come after us. We might achieve a recognition of the inherent right of self-government through constitutional change or accelerate progress in replacing the Indian Act with something more practical and more appropriate to the needs of aboriginal people. We might do so by eliminating the department of Indian affairs and replacing it with an Indian governments agency, an agency administered by aboriginal peoples not by government bureaucrats here in Ottawa, and one which gets its political guidance from an aboriginal assembly in which elected aboriginals can establish national policies on how funds will be distributed and how many of these problems will be addressed.
Unless we are prepared to think creatively about those kinds of changes then the mere appropriation of funds by Parliament directed through the existing kinds of programs that we can stand here and talk about will not solve the problem.
When the Prime Minister appointed me and shortly after the very challenging and significant summer of 1990 which we all experienced, when that was past the Prime Minister made a speech on October 24, 1990 to set out a new course of action. We called it the native agenda. Its purpose was to really create a new kind of relationship that would hopefully lead to a full partnership between First Nations people and all other Canadians.
One of the important aspects of that native agenda was that we would try to deal with some immediate problems. So the Prime Minister spoke of accelerating the settlement of land claims and unfulfilled treaty obligations. He spoke of introducing programs to improve conditions on reserve. He spoke of initiatives to develop a new relationship between the Government of Canada and First Nations, a relationship built on trust and respect. He spoke of trying to improve the role of aboriginal people in mainstream or contemporary Canadian society.
There were many initiatives that we took following those four themes: accelerating settlement of land claims, improving conditions on reserves, and developing a new relationship government to government. There was the constitutional process and the Charlottetown accord proposals. But we did not come with all the answers.
In fact, if self-government means anything to aboriginal people it means they cannot look to us and to this Parliament for all the answers, so we should not stand up here and give speeches pretending we know what all the solutions are. I will come back to that in a moment.
Where we did not have short-term answers, for the first time in the history of this country we set in place a process of seeking answers from experts to some of these most profound questions. The Prime Minister in May 1991 announced that we would strike a royal commission on the aboriginal question.
Rather than just striking a royal commission in the usual way and announcing who would be on it he said: "We will consult with First Nations leadership as to who should be on the royal commission and what questions it should address". He asked the former Chief Justice Brian Dickson to give some thought as to how to create this royal commission. That was the first time that the
March 10, 1993

Supply
federal cabinet and the Prime Minister turned the assignment of striking a royal commission over to an outside group. We will see in a few months time what kinds of positive suggestions will come from the royal commission to deal with the long-term question.
Let me mention what I told the Chief Justice when I met him before he submitted his report to government. I said that the fundamental question we must wrestle with is the question of the destiny of young aboriginal children growing up in Canada today: What will be their future? What can governments and their own people, their own leaders, do to help ensure a future of equal opportunity, equal quality of life and the right to have the same freedoms of choice in society as all other Canadians while preserving the aboriginal languages and cultures and traditions, which are so precious and important to First Nations people? How can we construct a better destiny for the children of the aboriginal peoples.
The first answer is that it is not up to us. We have something we can give and we must continue to give in material ways. However, if we lived in a remote northern community whose population was doubling every 10 years, surrounded by trees and with or without a road, and we were in a modem high school with computers and watching rock videos on television, what would we struggle with inside if we were a teenager thinking about our future? Would we want to get out? Could we afford to stay? If we stayed in that community without work, what would be our destiny? Would it be alcohol, other substance abuse or some of the other social tragedies we hear about?
The fundamental question is: What will be their destiny? I think we all have a responsibility.
I came prepared to talk about our progress on land claims and treaty issues. There is also the hundreds of millions of dollars in additional funds we have committed to increasing the budget for post-secondary education and to improving the sewers and water within Indian communities. There is the package before cabinet now dealing with an enhanced housing program for aboriginal communities and dealing with tragedies like Davis Inlet, Big Cove, and Fox Lake which is in northern Alberta.
I could talk about all the statistics and all the funds. The budget of my department is now more than twice as large as it was in 1985 and it is not nearly adequate. Each year we have had significant increases in our budget at a
time when all other government budgets have been frozen or near to that.
Assuming we can find the financial resources, the real question is the destiny question. It is important that we create a legal framework that is acceptable to First Nations, to native people where they no longer have to live in a sense feeling like subjugated people, subjugated to our Crown, to our laws, to our way of life, to our values and to our system which revolves around the dollar.
I hope the royal commission will give us some more profound wisdom. However, between now and whenever we find the magic formula we must continue to encourage increased levels of education. We must take away the shackles of the Indian Act and paternalism and create a climate where native people are free to risk, to succeed and yes, to fail in their own endeavours. And for their part, when they fail they should not come back to government expecting a solution.
I know we must be a caring society and a caring Parliament but we have to create a climate where social welfare is replaced with the freedom to choose, to succeed and to risk. We should help by providing education and by settling land and treaty issues and then by reaching out the hand of friendship. That is because I sense the one thing that has been lacking and which I find astounding is that in a country with 28 million people there has not been enough person-to-person bonding, where a First Nations person can say: "I really have a friend who is not of my own", and some of us can say the same. I will say that to the hon. member for Western Arctic whom I have come to know, respect, admire and feel great affection for.
When I travel across the country and in and out of aboriginal communities, I think it is such a tragedy that we really live in two worlds. Those of us who have so much to give expect government to do it and we are not prepared to reach out our own hand and offer help as we should.

On the first question about Metis and the recognition of Metis rights and claims, I think she knows that the minister for intergovernmental affairs has been given that responsibility as interlocutor for the Metis people.
The federal government has always wished to provide a proper recognition of the Metis people. They are in a category different from those of other than North American aboriginal descent and those who are full aboriginal. They are unique.
In the constitutional discussions, it was recognized that that uniqueness of the Metis people should be recognized and reflected in our Constitution. The recognition under section 91(24) should be accorded. With the failure of the Charlottetown accord or at least that stage of the process, that question remains to be resolved.
Meanwhile it is our view that where federal government dollars are transferred to provinces for health and welfare and educational purposes off reserves, provinces then have a responsibility to provide adequate programs for the benefit of Metis people.
Some provinces, for example the province of Alberta, have been quite generous in setting land aside and creating new communities for Metis people. I would not want to call them reserves because as I was saying in my remarks, a veiy unfortunate stigma goes with that.
March 10, 1993

In the case of the western Arctic, the hon. member knows that in the land claims process Metis people are being regarded as having equivalency to status Indian people. I think that is a step in the right direction.
I could not really speculate. I suppose it will take until after a federal election to come to terms with constitutional questions again. I could not speculate on how quickly that aspect of the Metis agenda might be advanced.
I just want to say in conclusion that we are all delighted to see Mr. Yvon Dumont named as Lieutenant-Governor of Manitoba. That is another measure of recognition of the important and rich contribution the Metis have given to Canada.
In regard to the Horton River DEW Line site, our government announced the $100 million Arctic Environmental Protection Strategy. I had the pleasure of making that announcement two years ago. One important aspect of that project is the clean-up of Arctic DEW Line sites and other unsightly dump sites across the Arctic. We are trying to facilitate these projects where local aboriginal people will do the work under supervision and at the same time get the best value for money so there is a competitive process of receiving proposals.
I cannot tell the hon. member for sure where the proposal she spoke of from the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation is, but I can certainly get her that material by way of a letter or report tomorrow.

decrease in the economic development funds available in the province of Saskatchewan for economic development on and off the reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question. The fact of the matter is that as with all governments these days, this government has a limited budget. The budget of my department has grown by $285 million this year. That is almost a 7 per cent increase. The budget of government programs for aboriginal peoples has grown $350 million, a 7 per cent increase on an over-all projected spending of over $5 billion.
Most government departments have their spending frozen. In the case of certain projects there are cuts of 10 per cent in grants and contributions for example.
It is necessary to decide how to preserve the important programs such as housing, where the funds were not diminished, such as education, where the funds were increased, such as welfare, social support, and child and family counselling. A decision had to be made about how we could fit within the budget.
In the final analysis the access to the treasury can only be had by the government on behalf of Parliament. Therefore it is not possible to have budgetary or over-all spending decisions the subject of consultation in advance. Funding for economic development this year will be $347 million, plus the funding of some $200 million in Pathways to Success.

March 10, 1993
Supply
The funding is not the problem, it is the management of the funding. We have created through alternative funding arrangements the flexibility for First Nations and tribal councils to adjust their priorities within budgets. If we reach the day where we see a transfer of global funding to an Indian government agency, then aboriginal leadership will have the delightful challenge of making decisions that would include cuts or rearranging priorities, which is the way it should be with self-government.
We want aboriginal people to control their own funding. That is why over 75 per cent of my department's budget is presently administered by First Nations people.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister spoke it was interesting to note that he made it sound as if whatever problems prevail today is the fault of the previous Liberal governments.
We have to understand that this government has been the Government of Canada for the last nine years. Its members keep blaming the previous Liberal governments for everything that goes wrong. They talk about how well they have treated the aboriginal people. They are now proposing, under the Department of National Revenue, to tax status Indians off reserve, which they previously never did. If the government does not reverse the decisions it has made on these issues, as far as we are concerned all this will be likened to a full-grown male caribou's droppings.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member thought I was accusing previous Liberal governments. I do not think I even used the term.
I was saying that a system of many decades duration which is based on the Parliament and the Indian affairs minister deciding what is best for aboriginal people, where we spend money to solve every problem, that that
system has failed. I said we are trying to turn in a new direction and establish a new relationship where we can make adequate funds available within the usual budgetary limits, but the difficult decisions and choices in future will increasingly be made by First Nations leadership. That is what I was saying.
I want to make it quite clear that the government has over $350 million available for economic development under the Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, and there is no 28 per cent cut in that amount. In fact, the government has increased significantly the funding for economic development. The results show that since 1984 we have seen the creation of several thousand new aboriginal businesses.
I should also point out that this year the funding for aboriginal education at all levels will be almost $1 billion. There are significant increases under this government which never occurred under previous governments in all of the history of Canada.
What I am trying to say to the House today is that all the money in the world will not solve these problems if the system is wrong. It is the system that this Parliament has to change.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to be able to participate in this debate both because of the substance of the motion before us and the very timely nature of its presentation.
I would like to compliment the member for Nunatsiaq for having the foresight to bring this motion before us. From what I have heard so far, I think the hon. members are certainly making use of this opportunity to put some very important points on the record.
I also appreciate being here to listen to the speech of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in this debate because after all he is the individual who most bears the responsibility for giving reality to the goals and aspirations of this House and indeed the Canadian people with respect to the aboriginal people.
The debate which has just preceded this, the discussion between the minister and hon. members with respect to what has happened with economic development cuts, indicates that in fact there is a problem, not only with the minister but with many participants in these kinds of debates at squaring the rhetoric that goes
Supply
with these kinds of issues with the realities which often accompany them. I would like to deal specifically with some of those aspects later on.
I agree with the minister that a new vision is needed in this country. Also I agree with the minister that the system as we have known it since the time of contact has led us down a blind alley. The system we know has led us to a situation where we have to deal with questions such as the epidemic of suicides in many Indian communities and certainly that is a trend we have to reverse.
At the outset of my remarks I want to pay tribute to the aboriginal families in this country. The motion before us says that this House condemns the government for abandonment of aboriginal families and children so this debate is really about aboriginal families and children.
In that context I would like to give credit and pay tribute to the aboriginal families that have touched my own life. I had the experience at the age of eight of coming into contact with people on the Beardy's Indian reserve, to get to know those families long before I knew anything about politics or issues or differences between people or the many kinds of dimensions to the whole question that one comes to later in life.
I very much value that childhood experience, the experience of Indian family life at its best.
In representing the constituency of Prince Albert- Churchill River, I come into contact with any number of Indian families in the course of my duties. There are 46 aboriginal communities in my constituency, including Metis communities, Dene communities, Cree communities and Dakota communities. I have had the experience of listening to the concerns of those families and of being able to experience their family life in a small way. To be able to have the opportunity of presenting the issues that arise from those contacts in this forum is certainly a rare privilege for any individual Canadian to have. Therefore I am grateful for that experience.
However when we are talking about what is happening to aboriginal families, it goes beyond simple issues of control, of funding, of parliamentary legislation and so on. It goes to questions of what is really happening to real families. Historically the record of what has hap-

March 10, 1993
Supply
pened to aboriginal families is extremely bleak. It is probably the darkest blot on the Canadian record.
We pride ourselves on being a peaceful, compassionate and sharing kind of nation, that we play that kind of role in the international arena. Certainly many people have developed the critique that before we get on a high horse and take too much pride in who we are as a people, we need to look inward at the historical record of the interaction between the majority of society and the aboriginal people.
Certainly it is not a bright record, not if you look at the whole situation of residential schools. There was a concerted effort, a comprehensive policy of alienating Indian, Metis and Inuit children from their own family heritage, from their own culture. It was a deliberate policy to assimilate the aboriginal people into the mainstream of society, no matter what the cost or what the consequences. We see those consequences on a daily basis today.
How could it be otherwise? We had two generations of aboriginal people who were tom from their family life, away from their communities, placed in an alien setting and punished if they in any way exercised their traditional ways, their cultures. After a situation like that, should we wonder why today we have problems of family breakdown, of alcohol abuse and of child suicide in our aboriginal communities. There is very little that is left to the imagination when you look at the historical record.
This was expanded by many of the social programs, the social policies that governments, both provincial and federal, exercised toward aboriginal people. One need only look at adoption policies, where it was considered a hallmark of progress to remove aboriginal children from their families and communities and to place them in white families far from their people, far from their culture and sometimes even far from their country.
What kind of a message did that send to the aboriginal communities? What kind of message did that send to aboriginal families, when federal and provincial governments had, as a matter of policy, the notion that it was best on a blanket basis for aboriginal children to be removed from their families and from their culture? That is part of the Canadian legacy that we need to examine. Certainly there has been a growing recognition of the abomination which this whole line of policy
development represents in our history. We talk a good line about coming to terms with these problems. We talk a good line about providing new resources and coming to these problems with new insights. But what is really happening?
Let me run through a very few specific examples. One is the Brighter Futures Program which the government has proclaimed with a great deal of fanfare. However that is all it is, a great deal of fanfare. Certainly we have all seen the press releases. The aboriginal communities have seen the press releases. As a result of that, the aboriginal communities developed proposals, very good ideas, on how to come to terms with the family violence issues, with suicide issues and with the abuse issues in their communities.
They develop proposals, think these things through, and set in motion a healing process in their own communities expecting that the government is going to make good on its word. Where is the Brighter Futures funding?
There is no such thing. There is no process by which people can access this money. There are no guidelines by which this money is distributed. This is a situation in which there seems to be a recognition of what the problem is but no way to access the resources.
In my own province of Saskatchewan in this very year, and in fact in the weeks leading up to the end of the year, $8.2 million will revert to the Crown, to the Treasury. This is money that was earmarked for family and social services for Indian people in that province. Those funds will be going unspent.
On the one hand, we have a situation in which there is a desperate need. It is a situation in which we have all kinds of ideas and proposals to perpetuate the healing process and to get it under way. On the other hand, because of jurisdictional arguments and the government having to prove a point, we have a case where if aboriginal people do not knuckle under to provincial jurisdiction they are not going to get access to the $8.2 million which they need.
The government is going to withdraw it at the same time as its members speak in the House to outline its commitment to dealing with these problems.
March 10, 1993

I just had the opportunity of participating in the discussion in the aboriginal affairs committee. The minister of Indian affairs appeared before the committee to outline his role in the settlement of land issues.
In talking about aboriginal families and communities one cannot separate those issues from land issues because that culture is fundamentally rooted in its attachment to the land. Its whole way of life and of viewing the world is attached to the land. We cannot separate these issues.
This is a situation in which the minister of Indian affairs is on the verge of introducing legislation in this House to create the Nunavut territory and settle the outstanding Inuit claims. All of us welcome the fact that those rights will finally be recognized and that a resolution of those issues is coming.
At the same time, the minister today took the position that the Dene people of northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba will be shut out of this process. These are families that from time immemorial to this very day have spent a good part of their time and made a good part of their livelihood from lands that are included in that settlement area.
This has been documented all the way back to Samuel Heame. At his first point of contact he found Dene people in those areas. There has been continuous use and occupancy. It was only after the policy began of moving Indian families to where schools and missions were that people did not continuously live in those territories.
Now the minister of Indian affairs says that if those families want to continue to exercise their treaty rights in that area he as the trustee is not going to do anything to help them. Instead, he is saying that these communities are going to have to go to the Supreme Court to exercise the rights that he is supposed to be protecting.
The minister is saying that families in those communities who are suffering from tuberculosis, malnourish-ment, alcohol abuse and a hopeless economic situation are going to have to take funds they should be using to meet their basic human needs in order to fight the minister in the courts. It is very hard to reconcile the minister's words with his actions when one sees cases like that.
Supply
As well, we have recently become very conscious of the whole question of suicide among aboriginal youth. It is very ironic in the international year of indigenous people that Canada's contribution to this whole discussion on the role of aboriginal people should lead off with the tragedy of Davis Inlet and the tragic situation of the young people there.
That is no different than what is happening in Big Cove or in the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation in northwestern Ontario. It is no different than what is happening in Fox Lake in Alberta or in Stanley Mission in Saskatchewan.
There is an epidemic of suicide in this country among aboriginal youth. But at the same time this is going on we are on the international stage saying that Canada is playing an exemplary role in the way it is treating aboriginal families.
It is quite ironic that in the very year we are doing that, on virtually a daily basis, we are being confronted with the fact that this is not the truth at all.
Another issue that I would like to raise is the situation of the Metis people in this country. In many ways the Metis people are the forgotten people of this land. They are the product of the interaction that happened between the European and aboriginal peoples at their first point of contact, which was the fur trade.
They evolved a way of life, a distinct culture and a unique language, which resulted in the Metis people being very central to the formation of the province of Manitoba in 1870. Indeed it was just one year ago today that this House very belatedly passed a resolution recognizing the role of Louis Riel in creating the province of Manitoba and thus contributing to the fundamental development of Canada.
It is timely that we again examine the role of the Metis people because when we look historically at what happened at the point of contact and what evolved out of it, the Metis nation, an argument can be made that in fact the Metis nation is central to the Canadian identity. The Metis have been the agents of change. They are the ones who best exemplify the issues that are involved in the contact between European and other cultures and the aboriginal people of this country.

March 10, 1993
Supply
Rather than having that role recognized, apart from a belated recognition of Louis Riel, the Metis people continue to struggle with the fact that they experience all the disadvantages of aboriginal life-the racism, the economic deprivation and the lack of access to their historical resources-while at the same time they enjoy very few of the benefits that accrue to people under treaty.
I recognize that there are tripartite agreements under way. Nevertheless the situation in Metis communities is extremely acute because for 100 years there have existed no mechanisms by which those people, who have been the harbingers of change in this country, can even meet their basic needs.
I would also like to turn to the issue of what happened in the recent estimates that the government placed before the House and in the economic statement that the Minister of Finance presented to this House in December.
As previous speakers have pointed out, there were some very startling numbers in those estimates that were presented to us. On the one hand, there was a 31 per cent cut in the Indian affairs budget for economic development. It was a cut of approximately $21 million. There was also a cut in the aboriginal economic program, CAEDS, which amounted to approximately another $6 million. So $27 million to $28 million was cut in economic development.
What does economic development mean? It means that people will be able to take control of their own lives. It means that the bread-winners in these families can provide for their own families. It means that there is hope for the future. It means that the aboriginal young people of today can envision a future in which they are contributing members of society and play a proper role in society. That is what economic development means. It means self-respect. It means self-reliance. It means pride and all those things.
What does this government do? It cuts those budgets, which would help lead to that kind of an outcome, by 31 per cent.
At the same time the government saw fit, and probably saw it was necessary, to increase the welfare budget by 12 per cent, by $52 million. The government says that it has
$52 million for welfare but in order to pay that it must cut $28 million in economic development.
I see that very phenomena in my own riding. I am not surprised. This year the government is spending $170 million in one riding, most of it on aboriginal people, for welfare costs and income maintenance. The elders and these families will universally say that welfare has been the ruin of the aboriginal nation. The welfare system as we have developed it has helped to ruin family life and has helped to ruin self-sufficiency. It has taken away meaning in life. The elders are unanimous in their condemnation of the welfare system as we know it.
Yet, what does the minister do? The minister perpetuates the welfare system while at the same time cutting drastically, by 31 per cent, the mechanisms that could lead away from that welfare state.
When questioned about this earlier he said: Yes, it would be an ideal state of affairs if the aboriginal communities were in the position so that they could reallocate this money from spending on welfare to spending on meaningful work and meaningful economic activity which would build up the communities. He said it would be a wonderful thing if that were to happen.
I would like to remind the minister that he has it in his power to make that happen. Rather than creating a situation in which that is going to happen the minister has gone the other way and without consultation perpetuated the welfare system for aboriginal families and drastically cut back their ability to do anything about it.
It is indeed true that not only this government but past governments and we as a Canadian people have in many cases and in far too great a way abandoned aboriginal families-Indian, Metis and Inuit families.
I would like to conclude with the point that not only do those aboriginal families need the support, partnership and assistance of all of Canada, but we as Canadians need the contributions of those families.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ABORIGINAL FAMILIES AND CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have found this debate today to be particularly interesting as it focuses on an issue that, through very sad events in the last number of weeks I have been forced, like all other Canadians, to come to grips with in real terms.
March 10, 1993

The situation at Davis Inlet that my friend from Labrador referred to earlier is a situation that has saddened Canadians and people around the world. It has brought many of us to the realization that these conditions exist in our country. They are conditions that many of us would not accept as being prevalent in 1993. For those of us who live in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and for people who live across the north generally, this situation is one we are reminded of often, and tragically perhaps not often enough.
At the end of January we saw some pictures that reminded us that children and families were suffering. They made us see a community that was having a great deal of difficulty in coming to grips with itself and with some of the problems before it. What is clear though is that this community, with the help of the Innu Nation, with the help of aboriginal people across Canada and with the help and encouragement of non-aboriginal people across Canada, is coming together to face the reality of the question.
Last summer, after a tragic fire in February 1992, the people of Davis Inlet decided in a report called Gathering Voices to look at the community of Davis Inlet, to look at the people, and to look at the families. They would try to judge for themselves what it was that was having an impact on their community, what the current conditions were that were having an impact on their children, what some of the historical realities were that led them to this position and this condition, and what some of the future opportunities might be. All of us, from time to time, are forced to look at ourselves and accept some hard realities. All of us from time to time should be prepared to suggest to ourselves that things need to change. The people of Davis Inlet went through quite a process. The reports that they have written, the comments that they have made and the talk about alcohol abuse, substance abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, child abuse and spouse abuse could not have been easy for the more than 460 people of Davis Inlet to talk about and to come to terms with. It could not have been easy to talk about it to the outside world and to write it down and publish it in a document that goes from testimony to commentary with photographs and poems and writings of young people and old people from today and from the past.
Supply
I hope I am not being presumptuous, but I think the report said that the healing must come from within. The report also said that the people felt that they could and must take that step and that the hope was there.
What also rings through, tragically enough, from the young people and from the children is that what drives them to the abuse and what has some impact on suicide is the lack of hope. None of us individually or collectively can live in this world without hope. They talk about nothing to do. They talk about an inability to see the future. They talk about the lack of hope.
Where do we go from here? Where does the community of Davis Inlet go from here? I think many in the country are aware that the Innu people of Davis Inlet were moved on to the island that they occupy today in the mid-1960s. I think many are aware that in the late 1940s the commission of the government tried to relocate about 75 people to the north. Two years later they were back in old Davis Inlet. During the first war when the caribou stopped moving through Labrador for a period of time, the people of Davis moved to where the trappers were and where the merchants were.
Today they live on an island in just under 100 houses that lack water and sewers. Many of the homes are in terrible repair and have insufficient insulation, roofs and foundations. Water is available from a central spout. It is not so much the physical condition of the community that I read about and the people of Davis that I talk to speak of. It is the culture, social relations, emotions and gut of the community that they are most concerned about because those are the future.
As we talk about relocating the community and the future of that community it is not again the physical movement of the community and what it will look like in terms of cluster houses or spokes. It is what that community will be.
The most important thing of the process that we are going through is to ensure the vision that the people of Davis Inlet have for their community. This will lead them to decide on how that community will work, to deal with the questions of how the education system will function and to see how health care will meet broad

March 10, 1993
Supply
family needs that deal not only with the substance abuse question but wellness and all that that means.
This is the vision that will incorporate the social fabric of the community where extended families have always been so important. It will take into account the cultural realities of the Innu, the Naskapi, the people of Davis Inlet and will address what the economic opportunities are for those people.
What are the things that in the future the children of Davis Inlet will do? It is that vision that must guide what this new community will be, how it will function and how the people of the community will relate to each other, to the community and to the people around them.
It is no good for the Government of Canada or the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador to go in and say, "We will move the community and this is what it will look like". It will not work. It is inappropriate and it will be ineffective.
We all want to ensure that we do not simply transfer the problems of Davis Inlet to a new community. No one feels that stronger about that than Chief Katie Rich and her councillors, the people of Davis Inlet, the Innu nation as a whole and certainly the governments.
What do we do? How do we avoid that?
First, we have agreed to tiy to reach an agreement on a memorandum of understanding. That will lay out an agreement on what it is we want to accomplish here.
Second, there is the process by which we will get there. Obviously there is community consultation and planning such as what went on last year around the report entitled Gathering Voices. That has to be an important part of that as does the funding.
The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, I think I can say without fear of contradiction, recognizes that it too has a role in this process and has a role financially.
The Government of Canada has made it very clear that it will support the process that will ensure the participation of the people of Davis Inlet and the Innu nation. More than the participation, it will ensure that the vision that I spoke of a few moments ago will be incorporated in every aspect of that community: education, culture, social relations, economics. That essence of
the community will be evident as they deal with the conditions that have led to the abuse and the tragedy we have seen around the children today.
There is more than that in the short term. We certainly have some situations that must be addressed immediately if those people are to live with minimal comfort over the next two or three years in the community that they presently occupy.
I have written to the chief and I have committed to her that we will provide the funding necessary to catalogue those needs and to look at some early solutions perhaps to some housing problems and perhaps to the provision of water. This is not to make big expenditures that will not be of any value to us after two years, but to ensure that the quality of life for the people that remain in Davis Inlet over the next little while is made a little bit better.
The question of health is particularly important to the community and for all of us that share the concern. There has been a suggestion that a wellness centre or a family well-being centre could be constructed. I think this is a good idea and I have given them the commitment of the government that we will with them do an assessment of what the health needs are in the community.
The nurses are in place now, the doctor that moves from place to place, the role of the social workers and the employees of the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador all have to be incorporated into providing the type of health care that ensures healthy babies, safe pregnancies and that the sick get the help they need and the aged get the comfort they need.
Help that focuses on preventive medicine and traditional medicine and medicine that reflects the needs of those people who have lived so long on the land in Labrador should be taken into account.
We are dealing together with the tragedy of the young children who are chronic abusers. They are now spending time in Alberta in an attempt to give them the support that is so essential and what they need.
The minister of Indian affairs and others have talked about ultimately changing governance in a fundamental way and the way aboriginal communities control themselves and have the decision-making power that they need so much. Self-government is a concept that has
March 10, 1993

been in this country for a long period of time. Some worry that it has no definition. Some worry that they cannot lay it down on a sheet of paper and follow it through. I understand that concern but it is not one that I particularly share myself.
To me self-government meets the concept of self-determination: responsibility for oneself and one's people. Self-government means that you have, as one of my colleagues today referred to, the ability to manage oneself and take the risks that are involved in that. It is to be able to ensure that the community says what happens to the community. The community makes the decisions not only in what it does but in the values that are the guideposts to those decisions. They are not values that are set or perceived in Ottawa or Vancouver or Halifax or, for that matter, perhaps Yellowknife or Whitehorse, but values that are of that community.
Because the history, the culture, the social conditions, the economic opportunities and the value systems change from community to community, the actual definition of self-government will change. Self-government for the Innu people and ultimately the people of Davis Inlet, or whatever term one wants to use, is the ultimate goal. The achievement by those people to be able to manage their present and therefore their future without the encumbrance of government but with the responsibility for themselves and their children and the responsibility over the resources that they will manage is something they want to attain. It is something to which I, this government and the members opposite are fundamentally committed.
The attainment of that is essential. It is an expressed wish of the people of Davis Inlet and the Innu nation that we reach conclusions on land claims in this area. I have given them my commitment. The minister has written that it is very much our interest to continue to pursue that.
We all recognize however, including the people in Labrador, that this will take some time. It is essential to me and to all the people I talked to that we not lose focus in dealing with Davis Inlet. We must recognize that the people of that community are our number one concern. The families, men, women and children of Davis Inlet can never leave our minds in light of land claims, the concepts of self-government and major and substantial policy issues that are on a national stage that
Supply
involve all aboriginal people and that must be solved and that do impact on the people of Davis Inlet.
However, if we are going to tie the success of the transfer of the community to the resolution in absolute terms of those issues, then we will never get to the problem of the people of Davis Inlet. This is a problem that they want to resolve and we have the obligation to work with them to resolve it. It does not mean that we turn our back on land claims, absolutely not. It does not mean we abandon self-government. Quite the contrary. It means that we look at things in context. We look at what is important, the people of the community.
In response to some very serious needs in the community we were able to provide some emergency short-term funding, quite substantial funding I might add.
We recognize the process that must be used by the community and the Innu people to reach agreement on the wording of the memorandum of understanding. It will lead us to the process of defining the new community based on the vision of the people of that community and is one that will primarily involve extensive consultation.
Yes, it will involve engineers, planners, economic experts and health experts. Even they ultimately must be prepared to respond to what it is the people of Davis Inlet feel will make their community work for them.
I believe absolutely that when the Davis Inlets of this country work for the people in those communities, they will work for every one of us in this country. They will work for all Canadians. As every Davis Inlet in this country becomes a better place in which to live, this country becomes a better place in which to live.
I believe absolutely that we together, led by the people of those Davis Inlets will find the solution so that the next generation does not go through this, so that we avoid that. We must be there with them to find those solutions.
